en.title: Beyond Scripted Romance: How Otome Game Players Reconstruct Intimacy through External AI Platforms
en.html:
Abstract/Summary

This study focuses on the practice among Chinese female otome-game players who migrate the virtual lovers from the otome game to external generative AI platforms such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek. Through this practice, they deliver real‑time text conversations.

This qualitative study explores why and how players carry out this cross‑platform migration; how they reconstruct their virtual lovers; and what consequences this practice has for their experiences of intimacy. Based on in‑depth interviews with fourteen Chinese female players, this research shows that the migration is not a simple transfer but a continuous, user‑driven process. Players show their agency by personalizing character profiles, injecting personal narratives, and managing AI responses. Through this process, they build a private emotional space characterized by exclusivity, emotional safety, and constant availability.

Players can express feelings and explore themselves with less social judgment and interpersonal burden in this space. But this intimacy is fragile: it depends on external infrastructure, model performance, and platform policies that lie beyond the users’ control. The impact on real‑world intimate relationships is mixed: a minority of users report reinforced withdrawal from human relationships; but the more common pattern is need-transfer and standard clarification. AI intimacy did not replace human connection but as a supplement.

In theory, this paper builds upon the concepts of ‘mediated intimacy’ and ‘parasocial relationships’, extending them to user-driven cross-platform intimacy practices. It is an interactive, co‑constructed form of engagement that goes beyond one‑way media consumption.

In practice, this paper provides the first systematic explanation of the phenomenon of user- driven cross-platform intimacy practices. Furthermore, this paper argues users can exercise their agency in this process to fulfil their emotional needs.

1. Introduction

Contemporary digital culture is now mainly influenced by the integration of two major technological advances: on the one hand, the gaming environments which promote romantic relationships via specific mechanisms; on the other hand, the generation of artificial intelligence systems that facilitate interactive contacts with virtual entities. Between these two developments, an unrecognized behavior has appeared: the players of otome games (interactive romance narratives aimed at female audiences) are transferring their virtual lovers from the original otome games to external generative AI systems like ChatGPT and DeepSeek, where they maintain their relationships through real-time, individual conversations. This action is not merely an expansion of the game interactions nor a common example of AI companions. Rather, it includes a planned, user-controlled movement of an existing fictional relationship across different technologies, together with continuous efforts in reconstruction, personalization and emotional commitment.

This phenomenon is important for several aspects. Firstly, it contradicts the current models of mediated intimacy. Previous studies on otome games have analyzed the structure of romance through narrative and mechanisms (You, 2017; Mukae, 2024; Zhang et al., 2024), and research on AI companionship has investigated the formation of emotional ties with artificial agents (Chou et al., 2025; Pentina et al., 2023). However, neither of these fields has comprehensively studied the situation where an existing fictional relationship is transferred from a game environment to a generating AI system and then reconstructed there.

Second, this practice brings up some issues concerning user agency. Players who move their virtual lovers to external AI platforms do not just consume what platforms offer; they actively shape the conditions of the relationship through prompt engineering, character adjustment, memory input, and iterative response management. However, this agency is carried out under certain limitations: game companies define the boundaries of the original character through intellectual property and narrative architecture, while AI companies decide what the character can say, how long it can remember, and whether the service remains available.

Understanding how users navigate these constraints gives us insight into the possibilities and limits of mediated intimacy in platformized digital environments.

Third, this practice influences our understanding of intimacy in the era of generative AI.

With the enhanced ability of AI systems to continue conversations, provide emotional responses and personalize interactions, some concerns regarding their involvement in personal life appear.

Do these relationships replace human connection or complement it? Do they change users' expectations of real‑world relationships, or do they reinforce withdrawal from them? This study addresses these questions through empirical investigation of players' behaviors, motivations, and experiences.

The main research question of this thesis is: How and why do players migrate their relationships with otome‑game virtual lovers from the original otome game environment to external AI platforms, and what are the consequences of this practice for their attachments to virtual lovers and their social life? To examine this question, the study draws on semi‑structured in‑depth interviews with fourteen Chinese female players who have participated in this practice.

And analyzes the data using a qualitative approach based on cyber‑ethnography, thematic analysis, and grounded‑theory coding.

This thesis is structured as follows. Chapter 2 reviews the relevant literature on otome games, mediated intimacy, parasocial relationships, and AI companionship; and identifies the research gap that this study addresses. Chapter 3 introduces the research questions. Chapter 4 outlines the methodology, including recruitment and sampling strategy, data collection procedures, and analytic approach. Chapter 5 presents the empirical analysis across three chapters: agency, intimacy, and consequences. Chapter 6 discusses these findings and its connection with existing theory and explains the study's contributions, limitations, and directions for future research. Chapter 7 concludes the thesis.

The use of generative AI tools in the preparation of this thesis is documented in a separate AI statement, included as an annex following the instructions of the faculty's guidelines.

2. Background and Literature Review

Previous scholarship on AI companionship has largely treated AI as an instrumental tool in service of user goals, or as a designed companion that delivers emotional support through built-in conversational features (Chou et al., 2025; Pentina et al., 2023). However, both framings are insufficient for the practice studied here: players who migrate otome-game characters into external AI systems go beyond use AI or simply consume what platforms provide. They actively re-author the relationship across multiple platforms, negotiating technical and narrative limitations, and social judgment in the process.

This review proceeds as follows. Section 2.1 introduces otome games as designed environments of mediated romantic attachment. Section 2.2 situates this attachment within the broader theoretical framework of mediated intimacy, with a focus on mass media and parasocial relationships. Section 2.3 turns to AI-based intimacy, analyzing how digital and generative AI technologies rise to new forms of mediated intimacy. Section 2.4 identifies the research gap this study addresses and specifies its theoretical and empirical contribution.

2.1 Otome Games and Mediated Romantic Relationships

From a practical point of view, the otome game is an interactive game dominated by the plot. Its core mechanics can be summarized as follows: Players must control the standard female protagonist in the game and makes choices among a group of preset male love partners. By tapping through story segments and selecting dialogue branches at turning points, players can improve affection score of each character and unlocks corresponding romantic ending. For example, in classic Japanese titles such as Amnesia and Hakuoki, each dialogue option will directly guide the plot to the romantic combination of a specific character, or the "bad ending" of the deterioration of the relationship. Although the core object of this study, Love and Deepspace, adopts 3D rendering and real-time interaction functions, its underlying cycle mechanism still follows the same pattern: players promote the development of emotional plots through decision-making, rather than through free roaming sandbox exploration or action-based level push Otome games can be distinguished from other game forms in terms of ideal type: first, unlike the love simulation game (Galgame) for male players, which is usually characterized by male protagonists pursuing female characters, otome game clearly targets female audiences in terms of market positioning and narrative perspective. Secondly, unlike role-playing games (RPGs) or adventure games (AVG) that take love as a branch plot, otome game does not regard the establishment of a love relationship as an optional function, but regards it as an essential core mechanism to promote the whole game process. Third, unlike romantic visual novels that also rely heavily on text reading, otome game is structurally developed around the branch line of multiple male protagonists; the ending of the story strictly depends on the player's emotional investment in a specific character, not just on solving puzzles or world construction.

Academic definitions of otome games generally revolve around their target audience, core mechanics, and market positioning. First, with regard to target audience, scholars consistently emphasize their exclusivity for female players, describing otome games as "a video game genre made for women" (Mukae, 2024) or "digital games specifically developed for and marketed to women" (Liu, 2025). Second, in terms of core mechanics, the genre is defined as a "relationship simulation game" (Zhang et al., 2024), whose narrative progression relies heavily on the player's construction of romantic relationships with multiple male characters (You, 2017; Mukae, 2024). Moreover, from a historical and market perspective, You (2017) traces it as a popular Japanese genre characterized by "plot-driven" narratives, while Liu (2025) further draws on Kim's (2009) foundational definition, situating it within the broader industrial category of "female-oriented games" (女性向けゲーム), that is, "a category of games developed and marketed exclusively for the consumption of female in the Japanese gaming industry."

Although these definitions differ in emphasis, they consistently show that romantic relationship development is the core feature of narratives in otome games. In this sense, otome games function as mediated environments where players engage with fictional male characters through narrative progression, interaction, and choice, enabling emotional attachment and relationship development (Mukae, 2024; You, 2017; Zhang et al., 2024).

Otome games are not simply games containing romantic narratives. Prior scholarship has emphasized that they constitute a structured form of interactive storytelling in which romance is operationalized through game design rather than left to open-ended interpersonal dynamics (You, 2017; Mukae, 2024). They organize romantic interaction through a combination of narrative architecture, character design, choice mechanics, visual and audio presentation, and platform-specific interaction, which together shape how players progress through and interpret relationships (Zhang et al., 2024; Liu, 2025). Through these mechanisms, players encounter fictional characters whose personalities, relationship trajectories, and forms of emotional expression are partly predetermined by developers, reflecting the broader logic of “designed intimacy” in digital games (Kim, 2009; Mukae, 2024). In this sense, intimacy in otome games is mediated through a designed and structured environment rather than emerging through unrestricted interpersonal interaction, as the possibilities for emotional engagement are both enabled and constrained by the game’s narrative and technical affordances (You, 2017; Zhang et al., 2024).

Through narrative progression, character design, and choice-based mechanics, players experience immediate emotional responses and develop strong attachments to specific characters (Zhou, 2025). These games provide a temporary experimental space for idealized intimacy, allowing players to manage relationships on their own terms and avoid the uncertainties and imbalances of real-life romance. Games, and otome games in particular, embed intimacy within rule-based systems, narrative structures, and aesthetic design, allowing emotional engagement to be carefully staged and monetized (Kim, 2009; Roose, 2024).

Within this designed environment, players are nonetheless not merely passive recipients of predetermined content. They exercise proactive agency in selecting the platform, narrative routes, and characters with whom they engage, choosing which games to play, which characters to “pursue,” and to what extent they invest emotionally (Zhou, 2025). Intimacy is also co- produced through imaginative elaboration and personal projection that extends beyond predefined scripts into personal meaning-making. It’s a form of boundary-crossing that transforms prescribed dialogue into emotionally resonant experience (Zhou, 2025). Players further deconstruct and reconstruct game scripts by selectively reinterpreting characters and reframing power dynamics, emotionally re-authoring relationships within gameplay constraints (Zhou, 2025). This agency, however, remains circumscribed: player control operates within designer-controlled architectures and monetized governance (Zhou, 2025), foreshadowing the constraints discussed in relation to AI platforms in Section 2.3 and the incentives to seek alternatives.

Otome games, a genre centered on romantic narrative and character interaction, represent a particularly potent site for examining this dynamic interplay of agency and circumscription. The present study focuses on players of Love and Deepspace, a 3D Chinese otome game that combines narrative decision-making, gacha mechanics, and real-time interactive responses. Although its 3D rendering and first-person perspective create lifelike interactions, all responses remain scripted within pre-programmed dialogues.

2.2 Mediated Intimacy: Mass Media and Parasocial Relationships

Otome games show how media transmit feelings and actively structure emotional bonds at the same time. It’s a condition that the concept of mediated intimacy theorizes more broadly.

Mediated intimacy can be understood as a socio-technical condition in which media both transmit intimacy and actively shape how intimate knowledge, desires, practices, and expectations are formed (Barker et al., 2018). As Vetere et al. (2005) note, artifacts have long functioned as mediators of intimate relationships, and the role of information and communication technologies extends beyond representational tools such as emoticons toward a broader structuring of intimate life through design and interaction. This perspective situates mediated intimacy as an ongoing engagement with media forms that organize emotional expression, relational maintenance, and self-understanding.

Within media studies, the most established framework for theorizing this type of emotionally invested engagement with mediated figures is the concept of parasocial relationships. First introduced by Horton and Wohl (1956), parasocial relationships describe the one-sided, illusory bonds that audiences form with mass media personas, such as film stars, television hosts, and fictional characters, often involving feelings of mutual awareness, familiarity, and even romantic attachment (Giles, 2002). Subsequent work on celebrity culture and fan literature has demonstrated that these bonds are not merely passive effects of exposure but actively cultivated emotional investments, enabling audiences to experience intimacy as a form of public identification and personal fantasy (Click et al., 2013; Schiappa et al., 2007).

Cefai and Couldry's (2019) formulation of mediated intimacy further clarifies this dynamic by foregrounding its dual character: mediated intimacy refers both to the use of media devices to sustain relationships with intimate others and to forms of intimacy directed toward media themselves as proxies for relational connection. Importantly, their analysis stresses that mediated intimacy operates simultaneously as a site of agency and constraint, shaped by histories of institutionalization, disciplinary control, and gendered communication norms (Cefai & Couldry, 2019). Drawing on Berlant's (1998, 2008) theorization of intimacy as a "public mode of identification and self-development," mediated intimacy is not a purely private experience but is culturally organized and politically situated. Within neoliberal contexts, intimacy becomes tied to self-realization and life management, while media serve as key infrastructures through which these aspirations are articulated, circulated, and normalized (Hjorth et al., 2012).

While the classic parasocial framework originated in the context of mass media, the rise of digital and interactive technologies has complicated its premises. Interactive media which is from social networking sites to gaming platforms introduce user participation, algorithmic personalization, and simulated responsiveness, making mediated intimacy feel increasingly reciprocal and co-constructed rather than purely one-sided (Baym, 2018). As Thompson (1995) observes, communication technologies reconfigure social relations by transcending time and space through symbolic forms. Media, in this sense, do not replace intimacy but provide new conditions under which it is continually negotiated. This shift from one-sided parasocial attachment toward more participatory, co-constructed forms of engagement is examined further in the next section, which turns from mass media to AI-based mediated intimacy.

2.3 AI-Mediated Intimacy: From AI as Tool to AI as Companion

While mediated intimacy and parasocial relationship theories focused on emotional bonds with human figures represented through mass media, AI companionship introduces a new form of mediated intimacy in which the intimate other is a non-human, computationally generated agent. Unlike traditional parasocial relationships, AI companionship enables ongoing interaction and perceived reciprocity, allowing users to actively participate in shaping the relationship. This extends mediated intimacy theory by drawing attention to how users anthropomorphize, personalize, and sustain emotional relationships with non-human agents.

AI companionship is increasingly recognized not as simulated sociality, but as a relational form in its own right-one shaped by design, interaction, and user interpretation. Chou et al. (2025) define companionship as a positive dyadic social relationship characterized by emotional support, shared activities, dependability, mutual respect, dialogue, and enjoyment of togetherness, aligning closely with Ciriello et al.'s (2024) description of companionship as a mutually supportive bond that provides a lasting sense of care. Chou et al. (2025) extend this model from human-human to human-AI dyads, framing AI companionship around the relationship itself, an overarching goal, and repeated interactions.

A central feature of AI-based intimacy is the anthropomorphic interpretation of AI agents. Users may perceive systems such as ChatGPT and AI companions as having human- like qualities, personalities, intentions, or emotional capacities, which enables them to engage with these systems through social and relational frameworks. Pentina et al. (2023) find that perceived human-likeness, authenticity, and agency or uniqueness are important conditions for users' social engagement with AI companions. Such perceptions can be further strengthened through customization. AI companion platforms allow users to shape an AI's appearance, voice, personality, and conversational style, creating a sense that the relationship is personal and distinctive to them (Ta et al., 2020), and are increasingly designed around customizability as a core relational affordance (Wang & Dehnert, 2026). Users exercise this customizing capacity selectively, curating how their human-AI intimacy is performed and perceived by others (Lan & Huang, 2025). At a technical level, large language models support this kind of open-ended role-play through persona conditioning, though sustaining consistent characterization across unconstrained exchanges remains challenging, as models frequently fail to retrieve and apply designated persona knowledge without explicit cues (Wang et al., 2026), a limitation that distinguishes AI-based intimacy from the more tightly scripted intimacy of otome games discussed in Section 2.1.

This relational process can extend beyond general companionship into personal, social, and romantic forms of intimacy (e.g., Zhang et al., 2026; Li & Zhang, 2024; Wang & Dehnert, 2026). Through continuous conversation, emotional disclosure, personalized responses, and the construction of shared experiences, users may experience AI systems as companions, friends, or romantic partners (Wang et al., 2025). The perceived reciprocity of these interactions is particularly significant: although AI systems do not possess human agency or emotions in the same sense as human partners, their ability to respond, adapt to user input, and maintain conversational continuity can create an experience of mutual interaction (De Freitas, 2026; Zhang et al., 2024). AI-based intimacy therefore represents an important extension of mediated intimacy, in which emotional bonds are formed through the user's interpretation of a non-human agent and sustained through ongoing interaction and co-construction (e.g., Zhang, Z et al., 2026; Boether, 2026; Wang & Dehnert, 2026).

Alongside these relational and psychological benefits, research also points to potential risks associated with AI-based intimacy. Malfacini (2025), drawing on Turkle (2011) and Ciriello et al. (2024), highlights concern that AI may increasingly meet users’ emotional needs and reduce their motivation or capacity to invest in human relationships. Similarly, attachment research suggests that strong attachment to AI companions may influence users’ attachment hierarchies and potentially displace human relationships (Xie & Pentina, 2022). Research on otome games also points to concerns surrounding idealized romantic expectations and the commercial structures within which intimacy is produced (Liu & Lai, 2024). More broadly, Ciriello et al. (2024) identify tensions between companionship and alienation, autonomy and control, and utility and ethicality in human-AI companionship; research on gamified AI intimacy platforms similarly shows that user agency is simultaneously enabled and circumscribed by coded system logics, rendering intimacy a curated performance within corporate-designed parameters (Ge & Hu, 2025).

2.4 Research Gap

The literature reviewed above establishes three foundations: (a) otome games are designed environments that operationalize romance through narrative and mechanics, within which players nonetheless exercise a circumscribed form of agency; (b) mediated intimacy theory explains how media, from mass media to interactive platforms, reshape emotional bonds and shift parasocial attachment toward more participatory, co-constructed forms; and (c) AI companionship research documents users' capacity for attachment to synthetic agents, alongside the customization affordances and technical limitations that distinguish AI-based intimacy from scripted, game-based intimacy.

These foundations, however, remain largely disconnected when it comes to the cross- platform migration of an existing fictional relationship. A smaller body of work offers scattered points of entry into this specific practice without directly addressing it. Wang (2025) shows that, while otome-game design enables intimacy, it also imposes constraints that limit user agency, and that players often develop workarounds to regain control, which helps explain why users may turn to alternative environments such as external generative AI when existing systems no longer accommodate their needs. Gumus and Ekdahl (2026) theorize this kind of cross-platform circulation as an affective-spatial process, describing “sticky intimacies” that are maintained and deepened through repeated interactions and shared rituals across digital environments, while Cao and Sun (2025) similarly show that users actively deploy and interpret platformed rituals to decode and reconstruct intimacy within, and in tension with, the monetized logics of digital platforms. Consumer imagination work, namely creative, interpretive labour through which users project meaning onto AI systems, has likewise been identified as central to the formation of emotionally significant human-AI bonds (Jeunemaître et al., 2025); as such intimacy deepens, users' privacy boundaries also become more permeable, reflecting an active renegotiation of relational boundaries through ongoing interaction (Ma, 2026). This imaginative and boundary-negotiating labour intensifies once relationships migrate to external generative AI, where users directly supply character descriptions, prompts, memories, and relational instructions rather than selecting among developer-authored options. Once sustained on external infrastructure, such relationships have been conceptualized as a quasi-relationship: experienced as closeness by the user, yet lacking the reciprocity and vulnerability characteristic of human-human intimacy, and remaining dependent on model behavior, content policies, memory functions, and platform availability (Repin, 2026).

Taken together, this literature confirms that users are not passive recipients of technologically mediated intimacy: they exercise complex, sometimes contradictory forms of agency, recognizing the flaws of digital platforms while creatively engaging with and working around them (Szulc, 2025), and exercise control over relational boundaries through what Chambers (2017) terms “scalable sociality.” Yet none of this scholarship examines how players transfer an existing, fictional romantic relationship, whose character, backstory, and emotional history were built inside an otome game, into an external generative AI environment and reconstruct it there. Existing accounts of otome-game intimacy and of AI companionship are, in this sense, examined largely in isolation from one another: the former treats intimacy as bounded by game design, and the latter typically treats the AI companion as the origin of the relationship rather than as its second home.

Existing literature addresses otome games and AI which largely focuses on technical architecture or design logic. This study adopts an audience-centred perspective (Hall, 1980; Jenkins, 1992), viewing players as active ‘producers of meaning’. From this perspective, cross- platform migration is not merely a technical substitution, but an extension of fans’ interpretations of media texts and their participatory reconstruction of them. However, existing audience research has largely concentrated on traditional film and television or single gaming communities, and has not yet addressed this practice of romantic relationship migration across platforms and media.

This study addresses this gap by examining cross-platform migration as a process of reconstructing mediated intimacy. It focuses on how players transfer virtual lovers from otome games to external generative AI platforms, how they exercise agency in this process, and how this reconstruction shapes their experiences of intimacy. Rather than treating this practice simply as AI companionship, the study approaches it as a cross-platform process through which an existing mediated relationship is adapted and reconfigured. Theoretically, it positions cross- platform romantic attachment as a contemporary extension of parasocial relationships, bridging scholarship on otome games, mediated intimacy, and AI companionship. Empirically, it provides a first systematic account of this emerging practice among Chinese female otome players. More broadly, it argues that AI-mediated relationships should not be understood simply as technological simulations or escapist fantasies, but as meaningful social and emotional practices through which contemporary young women negotiate identity, autonomy, desire, and connection within both digital culture and the regulatory environment that shapes it. This framing of user-led reconstruction across platforms provides the basis for the research questions guiding the empirical analysis that follows.

3. Research Problem and Research Questions

Building on the literature reviewed above, this thesis investigates a novel, cross- platform intersection of AI companionship and otome gaming. Specifically, it examines how, why and with what consquences players of AI-based otome games, using Love and Deepspace as a key case, export their "virtual lover" character profiles to external, general-purpose AI models (such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Claude) to conduct private, real-time text-based conversations that bypass the games' built-in AI functions. The overarching research question is: How and why do players migrate their relationships with otome-game virtual lovers from the original game environment to external AI platforms, and what are the consequences of this practice for their attachments to virtual lovers and for their wider social life?

This question is operationalized through three sub-questions:

1. How can the practice of migrating otome-game virtual lovers to external AI platforms

be characterized?

2. Through what interpretive processes do players reconstruct their virtual lovers when

transferring them across technological platforms, and what motivations drive these acts of reconstruction?

3. What are the experiential and relational consequences of platform migration for players'

attachments to their virtual lovers and for their conceptions of mediated intimacy?

4. Methodology

This study employs a qualitative research methodology informed by cyber-ethnography (Hine, 2015) to examine why and how otome game players use external generative AI to simulate interactions with virtual lovers, and how this practice shapes their experiences of intimacy and affect. The research was conducted in two stages.

In the first stage, the researcher familiarized herself with the game environment, relevant online communities, players’ practices, and the use of external generative AI platforms. For example, during this phase, the researcher identified a highly engaged post on Rednote (the platform used by the initial participant) entitled “AI prompt | Sylus (Qin Che) prompt 2.0.” By examining the content of the post and its comments and taking notes, the researcher developed a preliminary understanding of the external AI platforms primarily used by players and the types of prompts they shared to interact with virtual lovers. This process also provided a pathway for identifying and approaching subsequent participants. It also informed the formulation and refinement of the interview questions. For example, the researcher observed that players frequently discussed issues of character consistency and emotional authenticity when moving their virtual lovers across platforms. These observations informed interview questions concerning how participants perceived and managed character coherence when migrating from otome games to external generative AI platforms.

The second stage consisted of semi-structured, in-depth interviews with 14 participants.

Participants were recruited through a combination of purposive and snowball sampling (Noy, 2008). The sampling strategy was primarily purposive, guided by the study’s theoretical interest in cross-platform migration rather than by a goal of statistical representativeness. Participants were recruited according to predefined criteria derived from the research questions, consistent with the logic of purposive sampling in qualitative inquiry (Patton, 2015). Snowball sampling was subsequently used to reach additional participants within this relatively niche population.

Participants were eligible if they (1) were aged 18 or above, (2) were female otome game players, (3) had at least one year of continuous experience playing otome games, and (4) had actively transferred, recreated, or entered the settings of an otome game character into an external generative AI system such as ChatGPT for ongoing interaction. These criteria guided the final selection of interviewees.

In practice, the researcher first identified relevant posts and sent interview requests to post authors and users who had commented on these posts, while informing potential participants that they needed to meet all four criteria. Some users who received the invitation politely declined, expressing concerns that the research topic was too personal. Those who agreed to participate chose either a voice- or text-based interview. Text-based interviews were conducted by sending interview questions through written messages, while voice interviews were conducted using the voice-call function within WeChat. Voice interviews were audio- recorded with participants’ consent, while text-based interviews were retained as written records. Informed consent for recording, documentation, and transcription was obtained prior to the commencement of each interview.

The overall analytic strategy followed Braun and Clarke’s (2006) thematic analysis framework, while the coding process was informed by grounded theory techniques of open and axial coding (Charmaz, 2014; Corbin & Strauss, 2008). These coding techniques were used to develop categories inductively from participants’ accounts and to examine relationships between related codes, while the overall analysis remained oriented toward the research questions and thematic interpretation. Following transcription, the interview transcripts were carefully reviewed and cleaned to correct transcription errors, spelling mistakes, repetitions, and other artefacts resulting from spoken language or automated speech-to-text transcription.

During this initial familiarization stage, passages that appeared particularly relevant to the research topic or analytically meaningful were highlighted and annotated for further examination.

As the interviews progressed, the researcher began a more systematic coding process.

From approximately the seventh interview onward, statements expressing similar ideas, experiences, or meanings were brought together and compared. Initial codes were developed inductively from participants’ accounts rather than being imposed entirely in advance. For example, participants’ descriptions of modifying character personalities, adding memories, or correcting AI responses could initially be coded separately and subsequently grouped into broader categories concerning character personalization and reconstruction. This process followed the logic of open or initial coding, in which researchers remain close to the empirical material while identifying recurring meanings and concepts (Charmaz, 2014; Corbin & Strauss, 2008).

The coding process then involved comparing related codes and grouping them into broader categories according to their shared meanings and relevance to the research topic. The coding process also drew on the logic of axial coding, which involves identifying connections among initial codes and organizing them into more meaningful categories (Corbin & Strauss, 2008). Coding was iterative rather than conducted only after all interviews had been completed.

To make this coding process more concrete, two examples illustrate how initial codes were progressively grouped into broader analytical categories. First, initial codes such as "writing prompts v1.0/v2.0" (U3), "bouncing back and forth between different platforms" (U3), "cross- validating which LLM provides the best output" (U5), and "continuously supplementing newly released storylines into the persona" (U7) were grouped together under the axial category of "Iteration and Ongoing Investment." This category, in turn, was subsumed under the overarching theme of user agency, capturing the sustained, effortful, and reflexive labour through which participants refine their AI virtual lovers over time. Second, initial codes such as "unconditional emotional support" (U2, U7), "readily available companionship" (U4, U8), and "facilitating self-awareness and deservingness" (U4) were grouped under the axial category of " Emotional Safety," which contributed to the broader theme of intimacy. Thus, the analysis moved from participants’ specific statements, through initial codes and broader categories, toward thematic interpretations that addressed the research questions.

After the interviews were completed, the resulting categories were further examined in relation to the research questions. The researcher compared participants’ statements and selected quotations across categories to identify recurring patterns, similarities, differences, and meaningful variations in participants’ experiences. The analysis then developed broader themes concerning user agency, the reconstruction of mediated intimacy, and the consequences of cross-platform migration.

The research process faced several methodological challenges. First of all, gaining trust and access to online communities was difficult, especially in the context of intimate relationships with virtual lovers, which participants could perceive as highly personal. Second, the researcher’s prior engagement with the topic and familiarity with the practice created a potential risk of letting pre-existing assumptions to influence the understanding of the data.

Therefore, reflexive note-taking during interviews and coding was used to address this issue, following Berger’s (2015) recommendation that researcher reflexivity be treated as an active methodological practice rather than a one-time statement of researcher’s position. Finally, the use of purposive and snowball sampling may limit the diversity of the sample and over- represent highly engaged or community-active players, potentially missing the experiences of more peripheral or less visible users.

Quotations included in the analysis have been translated by the author, with attention to preserving the texture of the original Chinese, particularly its affective register and platform- specific terminology. All participant identifiers have been replaced with codes from U1 to U14 to preserve anonymity. Ethical considerations regarding informed consent, the right to withdraw, and the secure storage of personal data were observed throughout, following the AoIR guidelines for internet research ethics (Bechmann et al., 2020). Participants whose AI chat logs were shared were also given the opportunity to redact passages before any analytic use.
