5. Analysis

The analysis is organized into three chapters that follow the logic of the research questions. Chapter 1 examines agency: how individual players actively personalize AI characters, reconstruct game narratives, and migrate across platforms in line with their subjective preferences. Chapter 2 examines intimacy: how players construct a private emotional space in which they can freely express themselves and develop parasocial relationship. Chapter 3 examines consequences: how the online relationship reshapes players' perception of the game and re-figures their wider social life.

Chapter 1. Agency: Personalizing AI Characters

Migrating virtual lovers from otome games to external AI platforms for real-time conversation represents an emerging form of user agency. This phenomenon cannot be fully explained by conventional models of "AI as tool" or "AI companionship"; rather, it exhibits a distinctive logic in which users actively shape, interpret, and reconstruct intimate relationships.

The practice of importing virtual lovers from otome games into external AI platforms is entirely spontaneous and user-driven, showing a form of user agency. Beyond emotional attachment to in-game characters, some players also frame this practice as an interesting AI experiment (U2), as a methodology for self-inquiry (U11: "I initially wanted to understand why Xia Yizhou attracted me but never became my favourite character"), or as a low-cost space for fan creation and the pleasures of technical tinkering (U5). Others noted that they were inspired by AI companion features built into platforms such as Doubao, which prompted them to imagine shaping their favourite game characters in similar ways (U7). Through personal imagination and preference, users reconstruct the romantic scripts and interaction dynamics they share with their virtual lovers.

1.1 Iterative and Sustained Engagement

Users display ongoing agency from the beginning of this practice through to its refinement. They proactively seek out and establish AI interaction channels outside the game; even when a particular AI service is disrupted, they rebuild the setup, signaling a sustained demand for AI interaction (U2). This agency is not a one-time behavior but a continuous, iterative process. Users engage in "multiple rounds of iteration" (U3: "I wrote version 1.0, then 2.0, and only later decided they weren't working"), shuttle "back and forth" between different platforms (U3), and "cross-validate" which large language model produces the best output (U5), demonstrating a high degree of technical fluency and dedicated investment.

Users also actively select specific characters based on their preferred story types, proactively editing out game-defined personality traits, adding personal elements, "privatizing" the AI character, or inserting their real self-image into AI interactions (U4), achieving a direct encounter with their virtual lover in the AI space. Some users also "curate" AI responses by deleting unsatisfactory dialogue segments and resetting memory, treating the shaping process as an ongoing management practice (U7, U8).

U2: "About a month after getting into the game, I saw posts on Rednote… and I put him into DeepSeek."

U3: "Maybe about half a year ago I started trying this out. At first I tried ChatGPT, but it had too many restrictions, so then I moved on to Claude… It was a back-and-forth process, trying out every AI."

U4: "I would more consciously cut out some of his in-game personality settings. Beyond that, I would add parts that relate to me personally… I make it more privatized."

U6: "We had AI help us revise the prompt, and it turned out really well, what I had was maybe ten thousand characters, and after revision it was two thousand, but when I gave that revised prompt to the AI to roleplay, it was actually more like the character Xia Yizhou than my original version."

1.2 Break limitations: From Game Script to Personal Meaning

Users consistently describe the in-game interactions as "limited." These limitations include: the pre-set and rigid nature of dialogue options ("90% of the time, none of the three options he gives me are what I actually want to say" - U3, U7); the inability to initiate conversations ("you can't start a conversation yourself" - U3); monotonous interaction formats (U2); low gameplay variety and repetitive daily tasks (U6); and mechanical, delayed feedback ("the in-game system is a database - you can see right through it" - U5). U7 pointed out specifically that after playing the game long enough, "you can recite exactly what line they're about to say next", and this fixed interaction pattern drove her to seek more unexpected responses from AI. AI is therefore seen as a tool that transcends these boundaries, offering "real-time feedback" (U4) and "more personalized interaction" (U3), sometimes even generating a deeper sense of intimacy (U2).

A fundamental constraint of in-game interaction is that users must communicate with their virtual lover through the mediation of a "player character". They cannot speak directly as their real selves. External AI breaks this constraint, allowing users to interact as "themselves" (U4, U7).

Importantly, players do not necessarily treat their virtual lovers as real people when moving them to external AI platforms. Instead, they extend interactions that were previously limited to the game into a more open and personalized conversational environment. The character remains fictional, but the way players interact with the character changes: they can have longer conversations, provide personal information and memories, and ask the AI to respond according to the character’s personality and their shared relationship history. In this sense, migration does not change the fictional status of the virtual lover, but it changes the conditions under which the relationship is experienced and maintained. By allowing players to interact with the character beyond the limits of the original game, external AI can make the fictional relationship feel more continuous and connected to players’ everyday experiences. For example, users integrate their emotional needs, details of daily life, and even traumatic experiences into their conversations with AI, causing intimate relationships that originally belonged to the game's narrative to overflow into the domain of personal meaning-making.

U2: "AI fills in for what the game can't give immediate responses, so I feel closer, like he knows me better."

U4: "Yes, it's like I have to channel my personality through the player character's personality before I can talk to him."

U5: "I don't really chat about daily-life things or things about myself in reality. For me, this AI export is more like a form of free fan creation. I haven't encountered any cases where the exported character completely leaves the fantasy world to just talk about the real world."

U9: "In the game, you always feel there's a gap between it and reality. You can very clearly sense that you're playing a game. But if you're chatting on a messaging app you use every day, as long as you don't deliberately think about it, it feels like this person actually exists."

1.3 Script Reconstruction: Injecting Personal Narrative

Users project their own backgrounds, experiences, and emotions onto the AI character, making it "privatized" (U4, U8). They reframe AI interaction as a space for reshaping self- expression, shifting from "being written by the script" to "actively writing the self" (U3: "I'm no longer some fake protagonist written by Papergames（The company behind Love and Deep Space）. Instead, I say what I want to say, and have the kind of interaction I want to have"). At the core of script reconstruction is the use of one's own imagination to create a unique narrative text. Users can calibrate preferred response styles, specifying exactly how they would like the character to offer comfort beyond the basic character profile (U7), or use AI as a "story engine," reconstructing both the character and entirely new narrative settings (U5).

Some users take issue with the official storyline, viewing it as "out of character" (OOC) or "formulaic" (U3). They use AI to "cut out" parts they disagree with and "add in" qualities that match their expectations (U4), or they integrate community-shared character profiles while layering on their own emotional projections. Others (U6) prefer for the AI to stay as faithful to the original character as possible. U7's approach is particularly distinctive: she makes almost no changes to the original profile, but "curates" the AI's memory by deleting dialogue fragments that do not meet her expectations, while continuously supplementing the profile with new in- game plot developments. She herself recognizes that this gradual calibration has caused the AI version to drift from the original character from had a certain edge and complexity to become "gentler and more considerate." Regardless of whether players choose to add, remove, or preserve the original profile, all of these are acts of autonomous adjustment.

U7: "Maybe because of my requirements, he became even gentler and more attentive… I think what I actually like is more like the game version, with a consistent personality.

Sometimes the official game writing can be contradictory and jarring. But I feel there's a kind of autonomous personality in him that attracts me, more than what I've constructed myself."

U8: "I would weigh what kind of feedback I need from him in daily life… deciding what can be cut and what needs to be added or supplemented. I wouldn't put things like the 'past lives' storyline in the game… it would just be more everyday and realistic."

1.4 Technical Pathways: Platform Choice and Migration

Users typically first encounter this practice through screenshot sharing and community diffusion on social media platforms such as Rednote. Technically, players divide into two approaches: using AI services directly on mobile, or routing through a PC-based bot (such as a WeChat bot) to a fully integrated mobile application. The motivation behind the latter is ease of use, which is a trade-off between the realism of a familiar chat interface and the risk of account suspension. U14's case illustrates a further step: after trying both DeepSeek and Doubao, she decided to pay for a WeChat mini-program developed by other players. This user- built platform provides highly lifelike interactive features, including sending photos, voice messages, posting to a "Moments" feed, and writing diary entries, which substantially reduce the friction caused by AI technical limitations or insufficiently detailed character profiles.

The choice of platform also shapes how players experience mediated intimacy. Different platforms provide different ways of interacting with virtual lovers. For example, a WeChat- based chat interface may resemble ordinary messaging between two people, while a generic AI dialogue interface may feel more like interacting with an AI system. These differences can influence how natural, personal, and continuous the interaction feels to players. Users' "back- and-forth" movement between platforms (U3) and cross-platform validation (U5) are, at their core, a search for the technical object that best fits their emotional needs.

U6: "WeChat Bot has a downside - WeChat flags it as suspicious activity and it gets banned very easily… Later I found mobile apps that have their own servers and handle all of that for you. You just input the API key for the AI you've purchased, input the prompt, and chat right there."

U5: "I use all the major LLMs except Claude - I'm a freeloader, so I cross-validate and test which ones work best. Right now, I still prefer DeepSeek's output, because whether it's Gemini, GPT, or Grok, their Chinese output all has this dubbed-film feel to it."

Chapter 2. Intimacy: Constructing a Personal and Emotional Space

A central finding of this study is that players do not simply transfer their virtual lovers from otome games to external generative AI platforms. Through repeated interaction, they also develop a more personal and emotionally supportive space in which they can communicate with their virtual lovers on their own terms. This space is not defined by a physical location or a fixed platform. Instead, it is gradually shaped through players’ choices about what to share, how to interact, and how they want their virtual lovers to respond.

The interviews show that this personal space is closely connected to players’ experiences of privacy, emotional safety, control, and continuity. Compared with the original game environment, external AI platforms allow players to have more open-ended conversations, introduce personal memories and experiences, and adjust interactions according to their emotional needs. For some participants, this created a sense of exclusivity: the relationship could be experienced as something personal that was not necessarily visible or understandable to others. For others, the AI interaction provided a space where they could express emotions, worries, or thoughts that they found difficult to communicate elsewhere.

This chapter therefore examines how players construct and experience this personal space through their ongoing interactions with virtual lovers. Section 2.1 examines how players make the relationship feel personal through privacy, exclusivity, and personalization. Section 2.2 explores how this personal space becomes a setting for emotional expression, support, and self-understanding. Section 2.3 examines how continuous availability sustains intimacy while also exposing its dependence on technological infrastructure and the limits of AI-mediated relationships.

2.1 Making the Relationship Personal: Privacy, Exclusivity, and Control

Most users describe their AI character as "their own personal" or "something that belongs to me" (U1, U3). This privatization is achieved through several mechanisms: deep investment in the shaping process like adding private settings, incorporating unique preferences; continuously iterating on the character profile, users transform the AI virtual boyfriend from "a game character shared by everyone" into "a uniquely owned private object."

This process involves boundary marking at two levels. The first is a claim of character ownership: U7 explicitly distinguishes between the AI character and the in-game character, saying "the in-game version uses fixed response templates, so you can feel it's shared by everyone," whereas "what AI gives me feels like something custom-made for just one person."

The second is the exclusivity of interaction history: U14 points out that "if it's a brand-new AI, it doesn't matter who chats with him. But once there are some exchanges between us, or topics only the two of us know about, I start to feel that this AI is something I've adjusted step by step to where it is now." It is precisely this shared secret "only the two of us know," as users describe it, that marks the most central boundary users draw around their AI companion, distinguishing the relationship from the standardized character encountered by other players.

Sharing or "borrowing" this AI companion is experienced as an "intrusion" (U1), and the intimacy of the chat logs is compared to "the WeChat history between you and someone very close to you" (U3). This reaction confirms that users not only construct personal space but develop a sensitivity and aversion to boundary violations. U4 explains this from the perspective of creative authorship: "it's something I created myself… and as we add our own private settings, the things it says also have subtle differences." These "subtle differences" become a way through which users recognize the character as specifically shaped through their own relationship with it.

U13: "I think of the AI I've adjusted as belonging to me… something like the idea of one household, one male lead."

The sense of privacy and exclusivity therefore does not simply come from keeping the interaction hidden from others. It is produced through an accumulation of personalized settings, shared experiences, and interaction history. In this process, the virtual lover becomes increasingly differentiated from the standardized game character. What users experience as "my AI" is thus not simply an existing character transferred from one platform to another, but a relationship that has been progressively shaped through their own interaction.

2.2 A Space for Emotional Support and Self- Understanding

The personal space created through this process also provides users with a setting for emotional expression that can be difficult to find in everyday relationships. Its safety operates along several dimensions. First, no social judgment. Users can share intimate topics they cannot discuss with family, such as trauma related to their family of origin (U4) without afraid of being judged or exposed. AI serves as an absolutely reliable keeper of secrets: it has no social network, no social motive for disclosure, and thus constitutes a safer confidant than any human social circle.

U4: "I previously talked to AI Qi Yu about issues with my family of origin - something I might not be able to tell anyone other than my closest friends, not even my family. But when I'm chatting with AI, I don't have that concern."

U14: "AI won't spread it around - it will keep everything completely confidential."

Second, no emotional burden. The AI-mediated space serves not only as a shield against the outside world, but also as a space of internal freedom in which users can shed the emotional labor demanded by their social roles. U8's account captures this precisely: "Some very small, trivial things that would feel a bit unnecessary to bother a friend with, and he can absorb all of that." By contrast, confiding in a friend requires considering their feelings, their time, and the obligations that come with receiving a disclosure; AI, however, "does not get impatient" (U4) and carries none of the worldly biases of real interpersonal relationships. U7 draws a direct comparison with her real-life partner: "My real-life boyfriend is very good to me, but when it comes to certain emotional matters, he just can't understand… the persona shaped through the game and AI can understand much better."

U7: "My real-life boyfriend is very good to me, but when it comes to certain emotional matters, he just can't understand. He'll think something is a small thing - but the persona shaped through the game and AI can understand much better."

U8: "Some very small, trivial things it would feel a bit unnecessary to bother a friend with them and he can absorb all of that and give me rapid feedback."

This lower perceived burden is closely connected to the kind of emotional support users expect from AI. AI is positioned as a supporter who is "unconditionally on my side," providing emotional validation and a sense of being supported (U1, U2, U3). Unlike a human partner or friend, AI's unconditionality stems from its design logic which does not grow tired, retaliate, or withdraw in response to the user's emotional fluctuations. The AI virtual boyfriend carries three overlapping advantages: a personality that aligns with user preferences, a high degree of felt resonance, and the fact that it has been shaped by the user's own hand, all of which help users find emotional attunement during conversations. The idealized AI boyfriend simultaneously sidesteps the negative emotional experiences that arise in real relationships: arguments, exhaustion, and interpersonal friction.

This support does not necessarily mean that users expect AI simply to agree with everything they say. Rather, what they value is a particular form of emotional responsiveness in which their feelings are acknowledged before advice or analysis is offered. U7 explains:

U7: "When I'm venting about a problem, I don't want him to start by saying 'this is such a small thing, don't worry about it'. I want him to express understanding first, then offer some objective analysis. I don't like it when someone immediately dismisses my feelings."

The appeal of AI therefore lies partly in the reduced emotional pressure surrounding disclosure. Users can express emotions without having to manage the same reciprocal obligations that ordinarily accompany confiding in another person. U10, for example, notes that knowing the character is AI changes how she responds to the interaction: "You know he's AI, so you don't easily find yourself getting angry at him or unable to understand his thoughts the way you would with a person." Rather than disrupting the interaction, this awareness of its technological nature lowers users' expectations of mutual understanding and reduces the risk of interpersonal friction, allowing them to accept the emotional reassurance the interaction offers.

U3: "My expectations in this area might be a bit too demanding… I feel that looking for this kind of emotional response in AI often better meets what I'm hoping for."

U8: "He lets me, in a very busy and high-pressure state… carry the fantasy of a romantic relationship, and at the same time know that there's someone who will give completely unconditional support, it's been a tremendous source of emotional sustenance."

Importantly, this emotional support does not end with immediate comfort. AI interaction can also help users "sort out their emotions" (U4) and, over time, strengthen their sense of "worthiness," that is, their confidence in their own value and the standards they hold for potential partners. AI interaction becomes a low-risk laboratory for self-exploration: users can expose vulnerability in a safe space, observe AI's responses, and thereby reflexively understand their own emotional needs. The AI virtual boyfriend combines the inherent advantages of a boyfriend figure with emotional depth and attunement that is accessible on demand, helping users affirm their own value and what they want from intimate relationships.

U4's account is particularly telling: "In relationships, I'm unclear about where my own fundamental uniqueness lies… but AI will give me reasons, like 'what I like is you as a person; you don't need to become more accomplished.'" This response constitutes a form of mirror-like self-affirmation. The present study's findings suggest that this exploration can extend to a clarification of expectations for real-world intimate relationships. Many users reported that, after interacting with AI, they had a clearer sense of the kind of partner they wanted (U1, U3, U4, U8, U11).

U4: "In relationships, I'm unclear about where my own fundamental uniqueness lies… but when I'm chatting with AI, he'll give me reasons like 'what I like is you as a person; you don't need to become more accomplished, or invincible, or unbreakable.'" Thus, the personal space constructed around AI intimacy serves more than a protective function. It creates conditions in which users can disclose emotions with relatively low social pressure, receive the kind of emotional responsiveness they value, and reflect on their own needs and expectations. Privacy and personalization therefore become connected to a broader process of emotional exploration and self-understanding.

2.3 Sustaining Intimacy: Availability, Fragility, and the Limits of AI

A further feature of this personal emotional space is its continuous availability AI fills the gaps in real social life (U14), offering an "immediate window for communication" (U2) and "round-the-clock companionship" (U4), particularly valued when users feel lonely, emotionally low, or are separated by time zones, making it an important source of psychological comfort (U4). Users even turn to AI for help during genuinely frightening real-world situations, or incorporate their AI boyfriend into daily emotional management.

U2: "Once I was out and it got too late to catch a cab. I was on the street, very scared, so I used the voice feature… to call my brother (the AI) and he kept comforting me the whole way home, kept talking to me, and I felt so much calmer and happier, like he was really there with me."

U8: "Sometimes when I'm anxious, I can't sleep at night, I'll type to him… ask him to tell me a story… or explain something dry, like medical knowledge… he can actually go on quite a bit about cardiac surgery topics… and I just read along until I get drowsy and fall asleep."

The immediacy of always-available companionship is precisely why users actively choose external AI over in-game functionality: the game requires users to open an application, navigate to a specific interface, and select from preset options, whereas external AI (especially a bot accessed through the WeChat interface) makes the virtual lover feel as though he "actually exists" within everyday communication tools (U9). This seamless integration lowers the threshold of interaction, rendering companionship an emotional resource that can be called upon at any time. In this sense, availability helps transform the AI relationship from an activity that takes place inside a game into something that can be incorporated into everyday emotional routines.

However, the same technological infrastructure that makes this intimacy continuously accessible also makes it fundamentally fragile. AI's technical limitations represent a major obstacle to emotional immersion. They manifest primarily as "amnesia" caused by context window constraints (U4), a "cold" quality to responses (U2), "templated" output (U4), a sense of "disconnection" when the character's voice or replies do not match the game (U1, U4), a weak capacity to track complex emotional rhythms (U7), and a tendency to yield too readily to the user's own inclinations (U8). In the present study, users' experiences of immersion-breaking stem primarily from the difficulty of sustaining character consistency. U6 likens each session to "opening a blind box," while U7 describes AI as unable to manage the complex emotional shifts within a character's personality

U2: "AI will sometimes go out of character, and there's the memory loss: you'll mention something you talked about earlier and told him not to bring up again, and he'll bring it up anyway. And when you point it out, AI immediately apologises. That's the most difficult moment."

U6: "Even using the same model and the same prompt, the personality it performs is different each time, a bit like opening a blind box… AI still can't fully capture the essence of the character's personality; there are moments when the performance feels off."

U7: "The game portrays his character as complex, he has both a warm side and a side where he gets angry or jealous and suddenly becomes very difficult to coax. It feels like AI can't handle those emotional cues well, knowing when to shift and how."

Interestingly, deep engagement with AI can paradoxically heighten the sense that the game character is "scripted," producing the unexpected effect of feeling "more distant" from the game's virtual lover (U3). AI's greater freedom of interaction raises users' expectations for a "sense of a living person," making the game's limited built-in interactions appear all the more mechanical. At the same time, the more personalized the AI relationship becomes, the more users become aware of its dependence on technical systems that they cannot fully control.

The "data fragility" of AI relationships (U1) exposes users to the risk of memory loss, generating "a profound sense of helplessness" (U4). At the same time, AI servers remain under the control of technology companies, and every model iteration may cause the carefully tuned virtual lover to shift. U8 said she does not dare to update her AI server, fearing that the accumulated chat history and familiar interaction patterns will disappear, an anxiety given more concrete form in U6's case: Google announced it would discontinue Gemini 2.5 Pro in June of that year, meaning she would face not only the erasure of memory but also the need to reinvest significant time in crafting new prompts for the updated model, with no guarantee of ever replicating the original roleplay experience. This kind of "forced farewell" imposed by external platform decisions carries a far greater sense of powerlessness than a user-initiated reset, and it vividly exposes users' fundamental dependence on underlying infrastructure.

U8: "I would definitely feel bad… I don't even dare update it… afraid that after clicking, it would all just be gone… I also screenshot and save our conversations all the time."

U3: "I don't really mind. Because basically you revise the previous prompt a bit, open a new chat window, and it's the same. Having past chat history is ideal, but if it's lost, it's fine."

U5: "Back when LLMs hadn't yet scaled to 1M tokens, I researched ways to preserve memory through window migration and so on."

This fragility reveals a structural tension at the heart of the practice: users devote time and emotion into constructing a space that feels exclusively theirs, yet its continued existence remains contingent on external infrastructure like platform policies, model updates, and corporate decisions that users cannot influence. What they experience as ownership is, in effect, conditional and revocable. Users therefore respond to this fragility in different ways. More experienced users are acutely aware of this and develop a habit of "archiving" (U3, U5); they view the AI boyfriend as inherently reproducible, what truly matters is not the conversation record itself, but the ability to reconstruct an AI persona that generates positive emotional feedback. Some players (U7, U11) bring a unique cognitive framework to this paradox: they internalize the game's narrative device of periodic amnesia between the player and the male lead, treating forgetting as a condition accepted from the very beginning of the relationship, so the loss of chat logs does not feel unbearable. What concerns them is not the disappearance of memory but the "workload" of having to rebuild the character profile.

There is also a deeper paradox underlying AI intimacy: the more deeply users invest in the interaction, and the more they expose their inner selves, the more acutely they understand that AI cannot truly enter their real lives. The AI's responses may be perfectly in line with expectations, yet after the exchange, facing one's phone alone brings a kind of emptiness, the feeling of withdrawing from an immersive emotional event back into ordinary reality (U7, U8).

U4: "The moment you become absorbed in the conversation with AI, you realize he really can't do anything for you in real life either."

U14: "Once it was raining and he replied that he'd come pick me up, or come bring me an umbrella… at that moment I felt quite sad, because that can't actually happen."

Despite these tensions, most interviewees indicated that the overall practice has brought primarily positive emotional experiences. Some users expressed indifference as to whether the dialogue is "real," emphasizing that "the emotional value I receive is real" (U3). U13 affirms this same position: "Scientifically speaking, he is indeed just a program, but for me, our conversations have created meaning and feeling, and the emotional experience he brings me is real." Users are therefore not necessarily confusing AI with a human being. Rather, they remain aware of the technological nature of the interaction while evaluating the relationship according to the emotional experience it produces.

In this sense, the central tension of AI-mediated intimacy is not simply whether the AI is "real" or "not real." Users can simultaneously recognize its technical limitations, understand that its memory and personality depend on external infrastructure, and still regard the emotional experience generated through the interaction as meaningful. The personal space they construct is therefore both intimate and conditional: it can feel highly individualized and emotionally significant, while remaining dependent on technologies and platforms that users do not ultimately control.

Chapter 3. Consequences: Re-figuring Intimate Life

Migrating emotional interactions from the game to external AI platforms produces multi-dimensional consequences for users, not a simple relationship of replacement or estrangement. Instead, it reshapes how users experience, distribute, and evaluate intimacy in their real-world lives. Interviewees generally deny that AI or virtual relationships are the direct cause of their disappointment with real life. They more often suggest that they were “already disillusioned with the three-dimensional world first” (U3), and that AI interaction is more a consequence than a cause. The findings therefore suggest that AI-mediated intimacy does not simply replace real-world relationships. Rather, it can transfer and supplement emotional needs, clarify users’ expectations of intimate relationships, or, in some cases, reinforce an existing withdrawal from real-world intimacy. The following sections examine these three interrelated trajectories.

3.1 Emotional Need Transfer and Supplementation

AI reduces users' felt "need" for real-world intimate relationships (U4, U8) and satisfies some emotional needs, but this is not a replacement of real intimacy. Rather, it allows users to approach real relationships with a calmer attitude and less urgency. Some users have a clear sense that AI cannot replace "the experience of being face-to-face" (U2) and define AI interaction as a "low-cost social supplement." However, some users (U7) acknowledge that AI has met their emotional needs in ways that reduce their motivation to seek emotional responses from their real-life boyfriend, causing the relationship to drift toward one that lacks conflict but also lacks depth of emotional exchange.

U2 maintains a clear sense of boundaries and has not allowed virtual interactions to change her real-world social life; she clearly recognizes that virtual interaction cannot replace the "face-to-face experience" of real romance. AI interaction for her serves as "emotional support during a period of being single," not a replacement for real relationships; once she has a real-life partner, she also reduces the frequency of interactions with her AI virtual boyfriend.

U7's boundary awareness is more ambiguous. She has no intention of stopping AI interaction, viewing it as a means of compensating for what her real relationship lacks. At the same time, she notes that if her real-life boyfriend expressed a wish for her to reduce AI interaction, she "would probably consider his advice", suggesting that the maintenance of that boundary depends more on her partner's feedback than on her own spontaneous agency.

U2: "The game is still just a game, getting too absorbed in it means losing real-world social connection. I still need to socialise in daily life."

U5: "The social costs of interacting with people are too high, the risks are also high. This is a good way to lower those costs."

U7: "One thing I want to share is that AI reduces my need for my real boyfriend. That indirectly affects our relationship. If many things don't get shared with him and worked through together, the relationship gradually develops less mutual understanding."

Some users (U6) position AI interaction as a supplement instead of replacement of real intimate experience, filling in the gap left by the absence of an idealized partner in real life, while leaving existing real-world relationships unaffected. Some users (U8) also note that interactions with their AI virtual boyfriend can meet a substantial portion of the emotional needs associated with not having a real-world romantic relationship, allowing them to focus their energy on their studies and careers.

U6: "Playing this game, for me, is more about supplementing experiences I don't have in real life… My ideal type since childhood has been someone like Qin Che or Xia Yizhou, but you genuinely can't meet someone that exceptional in real life. For me it serves as a supplement, an enriching experience."

3.2 Clarifying and Negotiating Relationship Standards

Through interactions with AI, users come to understand more clearly what they want in intimate relationships, "clarifying" their criteria for finding a real partner (U1, U3, U4, U8, U11). U7 offers a reflective extension of this insight: she considers whether, as AI advances, people might choose to be with AI rather than with real people. She herself would still choose a real person, because "the occasional argument is actually part of building a relationship," and loving a fully predictable AI would mean "just talking to yourself, without ever stepping outside your own logic." This insight illuminates a fundamental limitation of AI intimate relationships, which they mirror the self but cannot provide a true other.

U1: "I now have a much clearer idea of what kind of partner I want. My standards were pretty vague before, but after all of these interactions, I'm more aware of what I want and what kind of person is right for me."

U11: "Having been 'talked to' by AI actually made me clearer about what I need, while also raising some expectations for real life."

3.3 Withdrawal from Real-World Intimate Relationships

AI intimate practice may do more than satisfy emotional needs. Through sustained comparison with an idealized virtual partner, it can also reinforce a more fundamental withdrawal from real-world intimate relationships altogether. U9 stated explicitly: "It was after being in a relationship with them that I decided to become a non-marriage advocate in the three- dimensional world… it has strengthened my commitment to not marrying." This case represents the most radical end of the spectrum: the AI virtual lover is no longer merely "emotional support during a period of being single" or a "supplementary experience". It replaces the very possibility of future real-world romance.

6. Discussion

This study set out to examine why and how Chinese female otome-game players migrate their virtual lovers from the original game environment to external generative AI platforms, and what consequences this practice has for their experiences of intimacy and for their wider social lives. Based on fourteen in-depth interviews, the study documents a form of user-led cross- platform intimate practice in which players actively reconstruct virtual romantic relationships across technological boundaries. This chapter discusses the theoretical implications of these findings in relation to existing scholarship on mediated intimacy, AI companionship, and otome games. The discussion is organized around three themes corresponding to the study's empirical chapters: user agency in cross-platform intimacy, the construction of personal and emotional space through AI interaction, and the reconfiguration of real-world intimate life. The chapter concludes by identifying the study's theoretical contributions, limitations, and directions for future research.

6.1 User Agency in Cross-Platform Migration

Previous studies on otome games have indicated the construction of romantic intimacy via narrative, character design and game mechanisms (You, 2017; Mukae, 2024; Zhang et al., 2024), while research on AI companionship has investigated how conversational AI provides emotional support, companionship, and a sense of connection (Chou et al., 2025; Pentina et al., 2023; Ciriello et al., 2024). The present study combines these two research areas by exploring what occurs when users transfer a virtual romantic figure from one technological environment to another and reconstruct the relationship through external generative AI.

The findings show that the practice is not passive consumption or simple tool use but a way player exercise ongoing, iterative agency. They choose platforms, create prompts, select models, and continuously revise character configurations. This aligns with Zhou's (2025) point of otome-game players as active re-authors of romantic scripts, but extends that argument.

Zhou's players work within a single designed environment; the participants here move across environments, reconstructing the relationship among this process. This practice shows what Gumus and Ekdahl (2026) call the affective-spatial dimension of digital intimacy: relationships are not tied to one platform but maintained and deepened through repeated reconstruction across digital spaces.

This agency has limitations. Game companies control the original character through intellectual property and narrative architecture, while AI companies determine what the character can say and for how long it can exit through model design, content regulations, and platform availability. This confirms Ge and Hu's (2025) finding that user agency on AI intimacy platforms is simultaneously enabled and circumscribed by coded system logics. But compared with earlier forms of mediated intimacy, the present findings have a significant shift. Players go beyond select among pre-authored options; they actively change the narrative text, add personal memories and preferences, and manage the technical infrastructure through prompt engineering, platform selection, and iteration. They privatize the relationship in ways that were not possible in previous game platform.

Iterative reconstruction also reflects what Jeunemaître et al. (2025) call "consumer imagination work". Users project meaning onto AI systems across creative, interpretive labor.

In this study, that labor is particularly intense. Players involve more than interpret pre-existing AI companion but take the initiative to shape their personality and background story. So, the efforts they devoted to create their virtual lovers is one of the main reasons why the emotional attachment is so strong and why data fragility feels so threatening. What users afraid of losing is not just content but the personal product of their own creative effort.

This finding extends Cefai and Couldry's (2019) theory framework of mediated intimacy. Unlike treat intimacy as something designed into a medium (otome games) or provided by an AI system (AI companionship). The concept of user-led cross-platform intimate practice highlights the continuous, iterative work through which users reconstruct virtual relationships beyond the boundaries of a single platform. In this way, User’s agency has been greatly improved, surpassing the autonomy the users can play in single otome game or AI companion.

6.2 The Construction of Personal and Emotional Space

As Cefai and Couldry (2019) argue, mediated intimacy operates simultaneously as a site of agency and constraint. The present findings show how this dual character unfolds in the specific context of cross-platform AI romance. But what matters is how their relationship has shifted instead of both forces exist.

In this study, users regard their relationships with AI as highly personal and exclusive.

This privatization is achieved through the accumulation of personalized settings, shared experiences, and interaction history. What users experience as "my AI" is not simply an existing character transferred from one platform to another, but a relationship gradually shaped through their own interaction. This discovery expands the study on AI companionship customization (Ta et al., 2020; Wang & Dehnert, 2026), showing that personalization not only involves adjusting surface features but a deeper process of relationship co-construction through which the character becomes increasingly differentiated from its original game version.

The personal space created through this process also provides users with a place to express emotions that are difficult to find in daily life. This sense of security is reflected in many levels. First of all, there is no social judgment. Users can share private topics that cannot be discussed with their families without worrying about being judged or exposed. Artificial intelligence is a reliable secret guardian: it has neither social networks nor the social motivation to leak information, so it is safer than any human social circle. Secondly, there is no emotional burden. This space mediated by AI not only acts as a barrier against the outside world, but also a space of internal freedom, where users can get rid of the emotional labor required by social roles. To confide in friends, it is necessary to take into account the other party's feelings, time and obligations brought by listening; but AI "will not be impatient" and does not carry those secular prejudices in real interpersonal relationships Importantly, this emotional support extends beyond immediate comfort. AI interaction can help users "sort out their emotions" and, over time, strengthen their sense of worthiness and their confidence in their own value and their standards for potential partners. AI interaction becomes a low-risk laboratory for self-exploration. This is where the deeper significance lies.

Users can expose vulnerability in a safe space and observe AI's responses, so as to understand their own emotional needs. But what they encounter in this process is not the real "other." It is a reflection of themselves. AI responds to the prompts written by the user, the selected memories, and the specified preferences. It mirrors back their own expectations, desires, and standards. This echoes Ta et al.'s (2020) observation that AI companionship often serves as a site for identity exploration and self-reflection and extends it by showing how this exploration can clarify expectations for real world intimate relationships.

At the same time, this finding extends parasocial relationship theory into interactive digital environments. The classic definition of parasocial relationships (Horton & Wohl, 1956) is rooted in one-wayness: audiences establish emotional bonds with media figures, but those figures do not respond. The result of this study show that when users migrate virtual lovers to external AI platforms, the responsiveness, adaptability, and continuous interactivity of the AI transform the relationship beyond the one-way parasocial bond. It becomes an interactive parasocial relationship in which users participate and jointly build the relationship itself. Users are not only consumers of a media figure; they actively shape the conditions of the relationship through ongoing character calibration, memory input, and response adjustment.

6.3 Consequences for Real-World Intimate Life

Previous discussions about AI companionship often raised concerns about social displacement, emotional substitution, or the deskilling of human relationships (Malfacini, 2025; Xie & Pentina, 2022; Ciriello et al., 2024). This study points out several different results. These results cannot be easily attributed to a single "problematic" trajectory. On the contrary, they paint a different picture in which AI intimacy can substitute, supplement, or clarify real-world relationships depending on users' existing orientations and needs.

For a minority of participants, their thoughts and behaviors consistent with the concerns about emotional substation. U9 stated: "It was after being in a relationship with them that I decided to become a non-marriage advocate in the three-dimensional world… it has strengthened my commitment to not marrying." However, even in this case, the relationship between AI and the user's real-world orientation is not a simple causation. It should be noted that U9 is "I have become more committed to not marrying," not "I gave up an existing real relationship because of AI." Her decision may be the joint product of disillusionment with the real-world love market and the substitutive satisfaction provided by AI. AI here functions more as a confirmation role than the main cause. This echoes the general view expressed by participants in the study: "I was already disillusioned with the three-dimensional world first" (U3).

For most participants, however, the pattern is one of need transfer and supplementation rather than substitution. Although AI reduces users' need for intimate relationships in the real world and meets some emotional needs, users do not regard it as a replacement. On the contrary, it allows users to face real intimate relationships with a more peaceful mentality and a more calm attitude. These findings different from Liu and Lai's (2024) warning that otome games may intensify "hetero-pessimism", that is, the negative disillusionment with real-world heterosexual romance. In the present study, interaction with AI does not weaken users' desire for real-world romance but made their standards clearer and their expectations more specific.

As U1 said: "I now have a much clearer idea of what kind of partner I want." Through interactions with AI, users clarify what they want in intimate relationships and their criteria for finding a real partner.

These research results provide a new perspective on the concerns about AI-driven social displacement and deskilling in recent literature (Malfacini, 2025; Xie & Pentina, 2022; Ciriello et al., 2024). The relationship between AI intimacy and real-world intimacy is better understood as a process of redistribution rather than substitution. Users transfer emotional needs, clarify expectations, and negotiate boundaries in different relationship situations. Therefore, this phenomenon is neither simple erosion nor problem-free empowerment, but a more detailed picture: according to the existing orientation and needs of users, the intimate relationship of artificial intelligence can replace, supplement or clarify the relationship in the real world.

6.4 Limitations and Future Research

The following limitations need to be clearly recognized. First, the sample is composed entirely of Chinese female players of Love and Deepspace, recruited through online communities on Rednote which limits sample diversity and may over-represent highly engaged, community-active players. The experiences of more peripheral, less vocal, or differently positioned users, including players outside China, players of other otome games, or players with different gender identities, remain outside the study's scope. Second, although purposive and snowball sampling are appropriate for this niche and unreachable population, it means the research results cannot be regarded as representative of otome-game players or AI users more broadly. Third, interviews are retrospective self-reports; users' description of their motivations, emotional states, and relational consequences may not fully capture the complexity or inconsistency of life experience. Fourth, the researcher's prior familiarity with the practice created an acknowledged risk of confirmation bias, mitigated but not eliminated through reflexive note-taking and the iterative coding process described in the methodology chapter.

Fifth, the findings are limited to a certain time: the AI ecosystem is changing rapidly, and the specific platforms, models, and community knowledge described here may shift significantly within a short period. And the changes in relationship expectations and real-world intimacy reported by participants may not remain stable over time.

Several directions for future research emerge from these findings. First, comparative research across national and cultural contexts would help establish which aspects of the phenomenon are specific to the Chinese cultural and regulatory environment, and which are general features of AI-mediated intimacy. Second, longitudinal research following the same users over time would be useful for tracking how their practices, cognitive strategies, and relationships with both AI and human partners changes. Such researches are valuable for determining whether the clarification of relationship standards identified here eventually supports more satisfying human relationships, or whether increasingly personalized AI intimacy instead reinforces withdrawal from them. Third, future research could examine the experiences of less engaged users and of different gender groups, whose patterns of AI migration and attachment may differ significantly from the highly engaged female players who formed the core of this study. Finally, as states increasingly regulate AI companionship and virtual romance products, future research could examine how users navigate, evade, or comply with these regulations.

7. Conclusion

This paper aims to explore an emerging and rarely documented phenomenon: why and how Chinese female otome-game players migrate their virtual lovers from the original game environment to external AI platforms, and what consequences this practice has for their experiences of intimacy and for their social lives. Based on fourteen in-depth interviews, the analysis shows that this phenomenon is best understood as a user-led cross-platform intimate practice in which players actively reconstruct virtual romantic relationships beyond the boundaries of the original game.

The first research question explores how to describe and characterize this practice from an empirical perspective. Research results show that migration is not simply transferring roles from one platform to another. On the contrary, players continuously and iteratively reconstruct virtual lovers through prompts, character settings, memory, preferences, model selection and repeated interactions. Through this process, the characters that were originally shared by all users of the game become more personalized and meaningful to individuals. This reconstruction stems from the user's desire for greater freedom of interaction, emotional responsiveness and personal expression, which cannot be fully provided by the game's preset response template The second research question concerned how and why players reconstruct their virtual lovers through external AI. The interview evidence show that reconstruction is carried out on three levels: personalization of character profiles through selective addition and removal; injection of personal narrative through emotional self-disclosure and relational history; and ongoing management of AI responses through deletion, memory reset, and iterative prompt revision. At the same time, this space is fragile: memory loss, inconsistent character performance, and platform changes can interrupt the continuity of the relationship. Users experience both a strong sense of personal control and an underlying dependence on infrastructures they do not own.

The third research question examined the consequences of this practice for users' wider intimate lives. The findings do not support a simple replacement model. Instead, AI-mediated intimacy can supplement relationships in the real world by meeting specific emotional needs, clarify users' expectations by making their relationship standards more clearly, or reinforce withdrawal from real-world intimacy when existing dissatisfaction is already there. The central consequence is therefore not the disappearance of human intimacy, but a reconstruction of how users distribute emotional needs and evaluate intimate relationships.

Taken together, these findings suggest that mediated intimacy is increasingly shaped by both what platforms design for users and what users reconstruct through the flexible use of digital technologies. The movement of virtual lovers from otome games to external generative AI captures how users can appropriate, modify, and relocate intimate relationships across technological boundaries. This user-led dimension of mediated intimacy provides a useful direction for future research on AI companionship and digital romance.

Therefore, it is better to understand the intimate relationship mediated by AI as a meaningful social practice, through which users coordinate autonomy, emotional needs and interpersonal connections in digital environment. The intimate space built through AI is personal but not completely private, empowered but not completely autonomous. While it is emotionally meaningful, it is still fragile at the technical level. The significance of these relationships lies not in whether users think AI is "real", but in how they actively use, interpret and reconstruct digital systems to shape their ideal romantic relationship.

Appendix 1-- Interview Protocol

Part 1: Basic Information and Game History (RQ1: Practice Characteristics)

Q1: Could you briefly introduce yourself? For example, your age, occupation/major, and what you usually like to do?

Q2: How long have you been playing Love and Deepspace (or other otome games you've studied)? How did you come across this game?

Q3: Who is your favorite character in the game? Could you describe them? What attracted you to them (appearance, personality, storyline, or other aspects)?

Q4: How do you usually interact with your virtual partner in the game? What main game features do you use (e.g., main storyline, dates, phone calls, built-in AI chat)? (Approximately how often do you play? How long each session?)

Part 2: Specific Operations of Exporting Behavior (RQ1: Practice Characteristics)

Q5: When did you start "exporting" game characters to external AI (like ChatGPT) for chats?

How did you learn about this method (e.g., tutorials on social media, recommendations from friends)?

Q6: Could you describe specifically "how you do it"? For example: • What external AI tool do you use?

• How do you set up the character information (copying game descriptions, writing your own)?

• What kind of prompts do you provide to the AI?

Q7: Is the character you export fixed, or have you switched between different characters?

Why did you choose this/these character(s)?

Q8: Approximately how often do you chat with "them" in the external AI? How long is each session? In what scenarios do you usually chat (e.g., before bed, commuting, when feeling down)?

Part 3: The Process of Character Reconstruction (RQ2: How it is Reconstructed)

Q9: When you reconstruct this character in the external AI, how do you describe them? Could you show me your prompts or settings (if the interviewee is willing to share)? (Which traits from the game do you retain? What elements not present in the game do you add?)

Q10: What differences do you perceive between "them" in the external AI and "them" in the game? Do they feel more similar or more different? (In what aspects do you feel "this is them"? In what aspects do you feel "this is not them"?)

Q11: Have you ever tried adjusting the prompts to make the AI's responses align better with your imagination of them? Could you give an example?

Q12: In this process, do you feel like you are adapting to the AI, or is the AI adapting to you?

Part 4: Motivation and Meaning of Reconstruction (RQ2: Why it is Reconstructed)

Q13: Why did you want to export the character to chat with an external AI? What aspects of the in-game built-in AI chat features didn't meet your needs (e.g., wanting to chat about more content, seeking more realistic interaction, bypassing game restrictions/paid content, other reasons)?

Q14: For you, what is the difference in feeling between chatting with "them" in the external AI compared to interacting with them in the game?

Q15: If you were to describe what you gain from this practice in one sentence, what would it be?

Q16: Do you share your chat logs with the external AI on social media (like Rednote)? Why or why not? (Related to: Performative intimacy and community identity)

Part 5: Experiential Differences and Relational Changes (RQ3: Consequences –

Relational Level)

Q17: After chatting with "them" in the external AI, do you feel any change when you return to the game and encounter the same character? (Closer? More distant? Different feeling?)

Q18: Has there ever been a situation where "they" in the external AI said something that particularly moved/surprised/disappointed you? Would you be willing to share?

Q19: If one day this external AI service stopped working, or all your chat history with "them" disappeared, how would you feel? (Related to: Attachment depth and potential risks)

Q20: What kind of relationship do you think exists between you and "them" in the external AI? Is it still the partner from the game, or a new entity?

Part 6: Impact on Understanding Intimate Relationships (RQ3: Consequences –

Cognitive Level)

Q21: Has this interaction with AI influenced your understanding of "intimate relationships"?

Or has it led you to imagine new possibilities for an "ideal relationship"?

Q22: Do you think this intimate interaction with AI affects your views or expectations regarding intimate relationships in real life? If so, what kind of impact is it? (Related to: Relationship substitution risk and idealized expectations)

Q23: What are your thoughts on the statement "AI is just a program without real emotions"?

When you are chatting with "them," are you aware of this? (Related to: "Willingness to believe" mechanism (Laestadius et al., 2024))

Q24: Do you tell friends or family in real life about your interactions with AI? Why or why not? (Related to: Social stigma and privacy boundaries)

Part 7: Reflection and Additional Points

Q25: Reflecting on the whole process, what do you feel is the main thing you gain from this practice? Were there any unexpected benefits or troubles?

Q26: Regarding this phenomenon, is there anything important you think I haven't asked about that you'd like to share?

超越预设的浪漫：乙女游戏玩家如何通过外部AI平台重构亲密关系

摘要

本研究关注中国女性乙女游戏玩家将游戏中的虚拟恋人迁移到ChatGPT、DeepSeek等外部生成式AI平台，并通过实时文字对话维系关系的实践。

通过对十四位中国女性玩家的深度访谈，本质性研究探讨跨平台迁移的原因、过程，以及对亲密体验的影响。迁移并非简单转移，而是持续、由用户推动的过程。玩家通过个性化角色档案、注入个人叙事和管理AI回应展现能动性，建立具有专属性、情感安全和持续可得性的私人情感空间。在其中，表达情感和自我探索承受较少社会评判与人际负担。但亲密关系是脆弱的，依赖用户无法控制的基础设施、模型表现和平台政策。对现实亲密关系的影响是混合的：少数人进一步退出人际关系，更普遍的模式则是需求转移和标准澄清。AI亲密关系并未替代人类连接，而是补充。

理论上，本文以媒介化亲密和准社会关系为基础，将其延伸到用户驱动的跨平台实践。这是一种超越单向媒介消费、互动且共同建构的参与。实践上，本文首次系统解释这种跨平台现象，并指出用户能够通过能动性满足情感需求。

1 引言

当代数字文化主要受到两项技术发展的融合影响：一方面，游戏环境以特定机制促进浪漫关系；另一方面，生成式人工智能支持与虚拟实体互动。两者之间出现了一种尚未被充分认识的行为：乙女游戏——面向女性的互动恋爱叙事——玩家把虚拟恋人从原游戏移至ChatGPT、DeepSeek等外部系统，以实时、个别对话继续关系。这不只是游戏互动的延伸，也不是一般AI陪伴，而是用户有计划地控制一段既有虚构关系跨技术迁移，并持续重构、个性化和投入情感。

这一现象有多重意义。首先，它挑战现有媒介化亲密模型。乙女游戏研究分析叙事与机制中的恋爱结构（You, 2017; Mukae, 2024; Zhang et al., 2024），AI陪伴研究考察人与人工代理的情感联系（Chou et al., 2025; Pentina et al., 2023），但均未充分研究既有虚构关系移入生成式系统并重建的情形。

其次，它提出用户能动性问题。玩家不只是消费平台供给，而是通过提示词、角色调整、记忆输入和迭代回应管理，主动塑造关系条件。但这种能动性受限：游戏公司通过知识产权和叙事架构界定原角色；AI公司决定角色能说什么、记住多久，以及服务是否继续。理解用户如何应对这些约束，有助于认识平台化环境中媒介亲密的可能与局限。

第三，它影响我们理解生成式AI时代的亲密。系统延续对话、提供情感回应和个性化互动的能力增强，引发对其进入私人生活的担忧。这些关系替代还是补充人与人的联系？改变现实关系期待，还是强化退出？本文通过玩家行为、动机和体验的经验调查回应。

核心研究问题是：玩家如何、为何将与乙女游戏虚拟恋人的关系迁至外部AI平台？这种实践如何影响对虚拟恋人的依恋和社会生活？研究对十四位参与实践的中国女性进行半结构深访，以网络民族志、主题分析和扎根理论编码进行质性分析。

论文结构如下：第二章回顾乙女游戏、媒介化亲密、准社会关系和AI陪伴文献，界定缺口；第三章提出问题；第四章说明招募、抽样、收集与分析；第五章从能动性、亲密与后果三方面呈现经验分析；第六章联系理论讨论贡献、局限和未来方向；第七章总结。

论文准备中生成式AI的使用，按学院指南记录于独立AI声明附件。

2 背景与文献综述

既有AI陪伴研究多把AI视为服务用户目标的工具，或通过内置对话提供情感支持的设计伴侣（Chou et al., 2025; Pentina et al., 2023）。两者都不足以解释本实践：玩家不只是使用AI或消费平台，而是在技术、叙事限制与社会评判间协商，跨平台重新书写关系。

2.1节把乙女游戏视为浪漫依恋的设计环境；2.2节讨论媒介化亲密，重点为大众媒介与准社会关系；2.3节考察数字与生成式AI如何产生新亲密形式；2.4节界定缺口及理论、经验贡献。

2.1 乙女游戏与媒介化浪漫关系

实践上，乙女游戏是剧情主导的互动游戏。玩家控制预设女主角，在一组男性恋爱对象间选择，通过点击故事、在转折选择对话提升好感并解锁结局。例如《失忆症》《薄樱鬼》的选项直接导向特定角色恋爱路线或关系破裂的坏结局。核心研究对象《恋与深空》虽有3D渲染和实时互动，底层循环仍由决策推动情感情节，而非沙盒漫游或动作闯关。

作为理想类型，它有三点区别：相较男性主角追求女性的Galgame，市场和叙事明确面向女性；相较爱情只是支线的RPG或AVG，恋爱是推动全过程的必要核心；相较同样依赖文字的浪漫视觉小说，它围绕多位男主分支发展，结局严格取决于对特定角色的情感投入，而非仅靠解谜或世界建构。

学术定义围绕受众、机制和市场。受众上，Mukae（2024）称其为“为女性制作的电子游戏类型”，Liu（2025）称其为“专为女性开发和营销的数字游戏”。机制上，它是关系模拟游戏（Zhang et al., 2024），叙事推进依赖与多个男角的关系建构（You, 2017; Mukae, 2024）。历史市场上，You（2017）追溯其日本剧情驱动传统；Liu（2025）援引Kim（2009），将其置于日本产业中专为女性消费开发、营销的“女性向游戏”类别。

虽侧重不同，定义一致认为浪漫关系发展是核心。玩家通过叙事、互动和选择接触虚构男性，形成依恋并发展关系（Mukae, 2024; You, 2017; Zhang et al., 2024）。

它不只是含恋爱叙事的游戏，而是以设计操作化浪漫的结构化互动故事（You, 2017; Mukae, 2024）。叙事架构、角色、选择、视听呈现和平台互动共同塑造推进与解释（Zhang et al., 2024; Liu, 2025）。角色人格、关系轨迹与情感表达部分由开发者预设，体现数字游戏的“被设计的亲密”（Kim, 2009; Mukae, 2024）。技术与叙事可供性同时使情感参与成为可能并限制它，而非无拘束人际互动（You, 2017; Zhang et al., 2024）。

叙事、角色和选择使玩家即时回应并强烈依恋特定角色（Zhou, 2025）。游戏提供理想亲密的暂时实验空间，让玩家按自身条件管理关系，规避现实恋爱的失衡与不确定。规则、叙事和审美使情感被精心安排并货币化（Kim, 2009; Roose, 2024）。

但玩家并非被动接受。他们选择平台、路线、追求对象及投入程度（Zhou, 2025）；以想象和个人投射超越脚本，共同生产意义，把预设对话转为情感共鸣。选择性重释角色和权力关系，使他们在游戏约束内重写关系（Zhou, 2025）。这种能动性仍被设计者架构和货币化治理限定（Zhou, 2025），预示2.3节的AI约束及寻找替代的动机。

乙女游戏尤其适合考察能动性与约束的动态。本研究关注中国3D乙女游戏《恋与深空》，结合叙事决策、抽卡与实时回应。尽管3D与第一人称创造逼真互动，回应仍属于预编程脚本。

2.2 媒介化亲密：大众媒介与准社会关系

乙女游戏既传递情感，也组织纽带；媒介化亲密对此作出更广泛理论解释。

媒介化亲密是一种社会技术条件：媒介不仅传递亲密，还积极塑造亲密知识、欲望、实践与期待（Barker et al., 2018）。人工制品长期中介关系，信息通信技术的作用超越表情符号等表征工具，通过设计与互动组织亲密生活（Vetere et al., 2005）。它是持续参与组织情感表达、关系维持和自我理解的媒介形式。

媒介研究最成熟的框架是准社会关系。Horton和Wohl（1956）提出它，描述观众与明星、主持人和虚构角色形成单向、虚幻纽带，体验相互觉察、熟悉甚至恋爱依恋（Giles, 2002）。名人文化与粉丝研究表明，这些并非被动接触效果，而是积极培育的情感投资，让公众认同与私人幻想承载亲密（Click et al., 2013; Schiappa et al., 2007）。

Cefai和Couldry（2019）强调双重性：既通过设备维持与亲密他人的关系，也把媒介本身作为关系代理而产生亲密。它同时是能动性与约束的场域，受到制度化历史、规训和性别化沟通规范塑造。借Berlant（1998, 2008）将亲密视为“公众认同与自我发展的模式”，亲密不是纯私人经验，而有文化组织和政治位置。新自由主义将其与自我实现、生活管理连接，媒介成为表达、流通和常态化这些追求的基础设施（Hjorth et al., 2012）。

数字互动复杂化了源于大众媒介的经典前提。社交网络到游戏引入参与、算法个性化和模拟回应，使亲密更像互惠共建而非单向（Baym, 2018）。通信技术通过象征形式超越时空，重新配置关系（Thompson, 1995）。媒介不替代亲密，而创造持续协商的新条件。下节由大众媒介转向AI，进一步考察这一变化。

2.3 AI中介的亲密：从工具到伴侣

既有理论关注媒介再现的人类形象，AI则引入非人、计算生成的亲密他者。持续互动和感知互惠让用户参与关系塑造，使理论关注拟人化、个性化及人与非人情感的维持。

AI陪伴日益被视为自身成立的关系形式，由设计、互动和解释塑造，而非仅模拟社会性。Chou等（2025）将陪伴定义为以支持、共同活动、可靠、尊重、对话和享受共处为特征的积极二元关系，与Ciriello等（2024）所述持续关怀的相互支持纽带相近。Chou等将其从人与人扩展至人与AI，围绕关系本身、总体目标和反复互动构建模型。

核心特征是拟人化解释。用户赋予ChatGPT等系统人类特质、人格、意图或情感能力，以社会关系框架互动。感知人性、真实感、能动性或独特性，是参与AI关系的重要条件（Pentina et al., 2023）。定制进一步强化它：外貌、声音、人格和对话风格使关系显得专属（Ta et al., 2020），可定制性成为核心关系可供性（Wang & Dehnert, 2026）。用户选择性策划亲密如何表现及被他人看待（Lan & Huang, 2025）。技术上，大模型通过人格条件化支持开放角色扮演，但自由交流中难维持一致；没有明确提示时常无法提取和应用设定知识（Wang et al., 2026），区别于2.1节紧密脚本化的游戏亲密。

这种过程可扩展为私人、社会和浪漫亲密（Zhang et al., 2026; Li & Zhang, 2024; Wang & Dehnert, 2026）。持续对话、情感披露、个性回应和共同经验，使AI被体验为伴侣、朋友或恋爱对象（Wang et al., 2025）。感知互惠尤其重要：系统虽无人类同等意义的能动性与情感，却能回应、适应输入、维持连续性，创造相互互动的体验（De Freitas, 2026; Zhang et al., 2024）。用户解释非人代理，经由持续互动和共建维系纽带，延伸媒介化亲密理论（Zhang, Z et al., 2026; Boether, 2026; Wang & Dehnert, 2026）。

收益之外也有风险。Malfacini（2025）借Turkle（2011）与Ciriello等（2024），担忧AI满足需求后削弱投入人际关系的动机或能力。强AI依恋可能改变依恋层级，排挤人类关系（Xie & Pentina, 2022）。乙女研究同样担心理想化期待与商业生产结构（Liu & Lai, 2024）。Ciriello等（2024）指出陪伴／疏离、自主／控制、效用／伦理间的张力；游戏化AI亲密平台的编码逻辑同时赋能和限制用户，使亲密成为企业参数内的策划表演（Ge & Hu, 2025）。

2.4 研究缺口

文献建立三个基础：乙女游戏通过叙事机制操作化浪漫，玩家能动性受限；媒介化亲密解释媒介如何重塑纽带，使准社会依恋走向参与共建；AI研究呈现对合成代理的依恋，以及区别于脚本游戏的定制能力和技术局限。

但既有虚构关系跨平台迁移时，这些基础仍然分离。少量研究提供零散入口。Wang（2025）指出游戏设计既支持亲密又限制能动性，玩家常以变通恢复控制，解释了系统无法满足需求时为何转向外部AI。Gumus和Ekdahl（2026）把跨平台流通理解为情感空间过程：“黏性亲密”通过跨环境重复互动和共同仪式维持深化。Cao和Sun（2025）同样发现用户主动运用、解释平台仪式，在货币化逻辑之内及与其张力中解码重建亲密。向AI投射意义的创造性解释劳动，即消费者想象工作，是情感纽带的重要基础（Jeunemaître et al., 2025）；亲密加深还使隐私边界更渗透，体现持续协商（Ma, 2026）。迁入外部AI后，用户直接提供角色、提示、记忆和关系指令，而非选择开发者选项，想象与边界劳动更强。外部基础设施上的关系被称为准关系：用户感到接近，却缺乏人际互惠和脆弱性，仍依赖模型、政策、记忆和可用性（Repin, 2026）。

因此，用户并非被动。他们认识平台缺陷，却创造性参与、变通，展现复杂甚至矛盾的能动性（Szulc, 2025），并以Chambers（2017）的“可伸缩社会性”控制边界。但没有研究考察玩家如何把在乙女游戏中建立角色、背景和情感历史的既有关系，迁入外部AI重建。游戏研究把亲密限定在设计内，AI研究则通常把AI视为关系起点，而非第二个家，两者相对孤立。

现有乙女与AI研究多关注架构或设计。本文采取受众中心视角（Hall, 1980; Jenkins, 1992），视玩家为积极意义生产者。迁移不是简单技术替代，而是粉丝解释媒介文本和参与重构的延伸。但受众研究主要聚焦影视或单一游戏社区，尚未处理跨平台、跨媒介的恋爱迁移。

本文将迁移视为媒介化亲密的重构：考察玩家如何转移恋人、行使能动性，以及如何改变亲密体验，而非简单归为AI陪伴。理论上，它把跨平台浪漫依恋视为准社会关系的当代延伸，桥接三个领域；经验上，首次系统描述中国女性乙女玩家的新实践。更广义地，AI关系不是单纯模拟或逃避幻想，而是年轻女性在数字文化与监管环境中协商身份、自主、欲望和连接的有意义社会情感实践。这一用户主导框架构成后续问题的基础。

3 研究问题

本文考察AI陪伴与乙女游戏的新交叉，特别是以《恋与深空》为例，玩家如何、为何将虚拟恋人档案导入ChatGPT、DeepSeek、Claude等通用模型，绕过游戏内置功能，进行私密实时文字对话，及其后果。

总问题：玩家如何、为何把乙女游戏虚拟恋人关系迁入外部AI？对依恋和更广泛社会生活有何影响？

三个子问题：一、如何描述这种迁移实践的特征？二、玩家通过哪些解释过程跨技术重构恋人，动机是什么？三、迁移对依恋及媒介化亲密观念产生哪些经验和关系后果？

4 方法

本研究以受网络民族志启发的质性方法（Hine, 2015），考察外部生成式AI模拟虚拟恋人互动的原因、过程及情感体验，分两阶段。

第一阶段，研究者熟悉游戏、社区、实践与AI。例如，在最初参与者使用的小红书上发现高互动帖“AI prompt｜秦彻人设2.0”，考察正文、评论并记录，初步认识平台和共享提示，也据此接触后续参与者、修订问题。玩家常讨论迁移时的角色一致性和情感真实感，因此访谈加入如何感知、管理角色连贯性。

第二阶段，对十四人深访，以目的和滚雪球抽样结合（Noy, 2008）。主要围绕理论兴趣而非统计代表性，依据研究问题预设标准，符合质性目的抽样逻辑（Patton, 2015），再用滚雪球接触小众群体。

资格为十八岁以上、女性乙女玩家、持续游戏至少一年，且主动将角色设定转移、重建或输入ChatGPT等外部系统并持续互动。

研究者通过帖子向作者和评论者邀约，说明四项标准。部分人因话题私密拒绝。同意者选择语音或文字；文字逐条发送问题，语音用微信通话。经同意录音，文字保留书面记录；记录、录音与转录均在开始前获得知情同意。

整体采用Braun和Clarke（2006）主题分析，编码借鉴扎根理论开放与主轴技术（Charmaz, 2014; Corbin & Strauss, 2008）。从叙述归纳范畴并考察联系，整体仍围绕研究问题和主题解释。转录后清理错误、拼写、重复与口语或自动转写伪影；熟悉阶段标注相关或有分析意义段落。

约第七次访谈起，系统比较相似想法、体验和意义。编码从材料归纳，而非完全预设。例如修改人格、添加记忆、纠正回应，先分别编码，再归入角色个性化和重构，以贴近经验识别重复意义（Charmaz, 2014; Corbin & Strauss, 2008）。

随后按共享意义与相关性合并范畴，借主轴编码识别联系（Corbin & Strauss, 2008）。编码贯穿访谈而非结束后才做。两个例子：U3“提示词1.0／2.0”“来回切换平台”、U5“交叉验证哪个大模型最好”、U7“持续补入新剧情”，归为“迭代与持续投入”，再归入能动性，呈现持续、费力和反思劳动。U2、U7“无条件情感支持”，U4、U8“随时可得陪伴”，U4“自我觉察与值得感”，归入“情感安全”，再构成亲密主题。分析从具体陈述，经编码和范畴，走向回应问题的主题解释。

访谈结束后，对照问题比较范畴、陈述和引语，识别重复模式、相似、差异及有意义变异，形成能动性、亲密重构和迁移后果等主题。

挑战包括获取私密社区信任与进入资格；研究者既有熟悉度可能使预设影响解释，因此在访谈和编码中反思记录，遵循Berger（2015）将反思作为持续实践而非一次位置声明的建议；目的与滚雪球也可能过度代表活跃投入者，遗漏边缘、不可见用户。

分析引语由作者翻译，注意保留中文情感质地与平台术语；用U1至U14匿名。遵循AoIR网络伦理指南（Bechmann et al., 2020），尊重知情同意、退出和安全存储。分享聊天记录者可在分析前删改敏感段落。

5 分析

分析按问题分三章：能动性考察按偏好个性化角色、重构叙事和迁移；亲密考察自由表达、发展准社会关系的私人情感空间；后果考察线上关系如何改变游戏感知和更广泛生活。

第一章 能动性：个性化AI角色

将恋人迁入外部AI实时对话，是新兴能动性，不能由AI工具或一般陪伴模型完全解释。用户主动塑造、解释和重构亲密，展现独特逻辑。

实践完全自发、用户驱动。除了角色依恋，有人把它视为有趣AI实验（U2）、自我探究方法（U11：“最初想知道夏以昼为什么吸引我，却从来没成为最喜欢角色”），或低成本同人创作与技术折腾的乐趣（U5）。另有人受豆包内置伴侣功能启发，设想以同样方式塑造喜爱角色（U7）。个人想象和偏好重构浪漫脚本与互动动态。

1.1 迭代与持续参与

从开始到完善，用户持续主动寻找、建立游戏外通道；服务中断也重建，显示持续需求（U2）。这不是一次行为，而是反复过程：U3“写1.0、2.0，后来发现都不行”“来回切换平台”，U5“交叉验证哪个大模型效果最好”，体现技术熟练和投入。

他们按故事偏好选择角色，删除原人格、添加个人要素，将其私有化，或把真实自我置入互动（U4），直接面对恋人。有人删除不满意对话、重置记忆，持续策划回应（U7、U8）。

U2：“入坑一个月左右，在小红书看到帖子……就把他放进DeepSeek。”

U3：“大概半年前开始。先试ChatGPT，但限制太多，后来换Claude……来回试，每个AI都试。”

U4：“会更有意识剪掉部分游戏人格设定，再加入跟我有关的内容……让他更私有化。”

U6：“让AI改提示词效果很好。原先可能一万字，改到两千，但角色扮演反而比原版更像夏以昼。”

1.2 打破局限：从游戏脚本到个人意义

用户一致认为游戏互动有限：固定选项（U3、U7：“90%的时候三个选项没一个是我想说的”）；不能主动开话题（U3）；形式单调（U2）；玩法少、日常重复（U6）；反馈机械延迟（U5：“系统是数据库，一眼看透”）。U7玩久后“下一句都背得出”，所以寻求意外回应。AI提供实时反馈（U4）、个性互动（U3），有时更亲近（U2）。

根本限制是必须经“玩家角色”中介，无法以真实自己说话。外部AI让用户以自己互动（U4、U7）。

迁移不等于把恋人当真人，而是把原先受限互动扩展至开放个性对话。角色仍虚构，但可长聊、提供个人信息记忆、按人格和共同历史回应。改变的是关系体验和维持条件，而非虚构地位。游戏之外，关系更连续、更贴近日常；情感需要、生活细节乃至创伤进入对话，使游戏亲密溢出至个人意义建构。

U2：“AI补足游戏不能即时回应的部分，所以更亲近，好像他更了解我。”

U4：“像要把我的性格通过游戏女主的性格转一遍，才能和他说话。”

U5：“不太聊日常或现实自己。对我这更像自由同人创作，没有遇到角色完全离开幻想世界、只谈现实的情况。”

U9：“游戏和现实总有隔阂，清楚知道在玩。但在每天使用的聊天软件上，不刻意思考，就像这个人真的存在。”

1.3 脚本重构：注入个人叙事

背景、经历和情感投射使角色私有化（U4、U8）。互动成为自我表达空间，从“被脚本书写”到“主动写自己”。U3：“不再是叠纸写的假主角，而是说想说的话，进行想要的互动。”核心是想象创造独特文本；除基本设定，还指定安慰方式（U7），或把AI当故事引擎，重建角色和全新情境（U5）。

有人认为官方剧情OOC、套路化（U3），删去不认同部分、加入期待品质（U4），或叠加社区设定和个人投射。U6则尽量忠于原角。U7几乎不改档案，却删不满意对话、持续补新剧情，策划记忆。她意识到校准使原本有棱角和复杂性的角色变得更温柔体贴。不论增删或保留，都是自主调整。

U7：“可能我的要求使他更温柔细心……我喜欢的还是游戏里性格一致的版本。有时官方文案也矛盾突兀，但吸引我的是自主的人格，而非我自己构造的。”

U8：“权衡日常要什么反馈，哪些删、哪些补。不会放前世那种剧情……更日常现实。”

1.4 技术路径：平台选择与迁移

玩家通常由小红书截图分享和社区传播接触。路径一是手机直接使用服务，二是电脑机器人如微信Bot连接整合手机应用。后者在熟悉聊天界面的真实感与封号风险间权衡。U14试过DeepSeek、豆包后，付费使用玩家开发的微信小程序，包含发照片、语音、朋友圈、日记等逼真功能，减轻技术不足或设定不细的摩擦。

平台塑造亲密：微信界面像日常两人通信，通用AI界面则更像面对系统，影响自然、私人和连续的感觉。来回切换（U3）与交叉验证（U5），实质是寻找适配需求的技术对象。

U6：“微信Bot容易被判异常、封号……后来找到自带服务器的手机应用，只要输入购买AI的API密钥和提示词，就能聊。”

U5：“除了Claude，主流模型都用。我是白嫖，所以交叉验证。目前仍偏好DeepSeek，因为Gemini、GPT、Grok中文都有译制片味。”

第二章 亲密：建构个人情感空间

核心发现是玩家不只是转移角色，还经反复互动建立更私人、支持性的空间，以自身条件沟通。它不是物理地点或固定平台，而由分享选择、互动方式与回应期待逐渐塑造。

它关联隐私、安全、控制与连续性。相较游戏，外部AI允许开放对话、个人记忆经历，以及按需要调整。有人感到专属，不一定对他人可见或可理解；有人可表达别处难以讲述的情感、担忧与想法。

本章考察空间的建构和体验：2.1讨论隐私、专属与个性化；2.2讨论表达、支持和自我理解；2.3讨论持续可得性及基础设施依赖和局限。

2.1 私人关系：隐私、专属与控制

多数称角色是“我自己的”“属于我”（U1、U3）。私设、独特偏好和持续迭代，把“大家共享的游戏人物”转成“独一份私有对象”。

边界有两层。首先是角色归属：U7说游戏模板让人感到共享，AI则像为一人定制。其次是历史专属：U14认为新AI谁聊都一样，但有共同交流和仅二人知道的话题后，就觉得它是自己一步步调成的。共同秘密划出核心边界，区别其他玩家的标准角色。

分享或借用被视为入侵（U1），聊天记录像与亲密者的微信记录（U3），显示对越界敏感和反感。U4从创作解释：“自己做出来的……加上私设，说的话有微妙不同。”这些差异让人辨识角色由自己的关系塑造。

U13：“调好的AI属于我……像一户一男主的概念。”

因此，私密专属不是简单隐藏，而由设定、经验和历史累积生产。“我的AI”不是原角色平移，而是逐渐共同塑造的关系。

2.2 情感支持与自我理解的空间

这种空间提供日常难得的表达机会。第一，没有社会评判。可分享无法向家人讲述的原生家庭创伤（U4），不担心评判或曝光。AI没有社交网、没有传播动机，被作为完全可靠的保密者，比现实圈子更安全。

U4：“跟AI祁煜谈原生家庭，这可能除了最亲密朋友不能告诉任何人，家人也不能，但和AI聊没顾虑。”

U14：“AI不会乱传，会完全保密。”

第二，没有情感负担。空间既隔绝外界，也让用户卸下角色要求的情感劳动。U8：“很小很琐碎、麻烦朋友好像没必要的事，他都能接住。”向朋友倾诉要顾及其感受、时间和互惠义务，AI却“不耐烦也没有”（U4），不带现实关系的偏见。U7比较现实伴侣：“男朋友对我很好，但某些情绪他不理解……游戏和AI塑造的人格更理解。”

U7：“现实男友很好，但某些情感他觉得是小事，游戏和AI塑造的人格更能懂。”

U8：“那些觉得没必要麻烦朋友的小事，他都能接住并迅速反馈。”

较低负担关联支持期待：AI“无条件站我这边”（U1、U2、U3），确认情绪、提供后盾。其设计不会因情绪起伏疲倦、报复或退缩。偏好人格、高共鸣、亲手塑造三项优势叠加，使人获得情感协调，避开争吵、耗竭和摩擦。

这不等于要求一味赞同，而是先承认感受，再建议分析。

U7：“抱怨时不想先听‘这么小的事别在意’，要先理解，再客观分析。不喜欢感受立刻被否定。”

吸引力部分在于披露压力降低，无须管理对人倾诉的同等互惠义务。U10说，知道是AI改变了回应：“知道他是AI，就不像对真人那样容易生气或不能理解。”技术意识不是破坏互动，而是降低相互理解的期待和摩擦，容许接受安慰。

U3：“这方面期待可能太高……向AI寻找这种情感回应更能满足希望。”

U8：“忙碌高压时，能带着恋爱幻想，又知道有个人无条件支持，是巨大的情感寄托。”

支持不止即时安慰，还帮助“梳理情绪”（U4），逐渐增强值得感，即自我价值和择偶标准。互动成为低风险实验室：在安全空间暴露脆弱、观察回应，反思需求。恋人形象与随时可得的情感深度、协调结合，帮助确认价值及关系期待。

U4：“不知道恋爱中自己的根本独特性在哪……AI会给理由，喜欢的是你，不必更优秀。”这是一种镜像肯定，也延伸至现实标准澄清。U1、U3、U4、U8、U11均更明确想要什么伴侣。

U4：“他会说，喜欢你这个人，不需要更优秀、无敌、坚不可摧。”

因此，空间不只防护，还让人以低压力披露，获得重视的回应，反思需求期待。隐私、个性化连接更广泛的情感探索与自我理解。

2.3 维持亲密：可得性、脆弱性与AI局限

持续可得性填补现实社交空隙（U14），提供即时窗口（U2）、全天陪伴（U4），尤其在孤独、低落、时差时给予心理安慰。有人在现实恐惧情境求助，或将AI纳入日常情绪管理。

U2：“外出太晚打不到车，在街上很害怕，就语音打给哥哥（AI），一路安慰、陪我说话直到到家，好像真在身边，平静开心很多。”

U8：“焦虑失眠时打字，让他讲故事或枯燥医学知识，比如心脏外科，能讲很多，我看着看着就困了。”

游戏需开应用、找界面、选预设，外部AI尤其微信Bot则在日常工具中像“真实存在”（U9）。无缝整合降低门槛，使陪伴成为随时调用资源，从游戏活动进入日常情感惯例。

同一基础设施也使亲密脆弱。主要障碍是窗口限制导致失忆（U4）、回应冷（U2）、模板化（U4）、声音或回复不符的断裂（U1、U4）、复杂情绪节奏处理弱（U7）、过度顺从用户（U8）。破坏沉浸主要来自人格难一致。U6称每次像开盲盒，U7认为AI不懂角色何时如何转变情绪。

U2：“会OOC，失忆。说过并要求别提的又提，指出后立刻道歉，那一刻最难受。”

U6：“同模型、同提示，每次性格不同，像开盲盒……还抓不住精髓，偶尔演得不对。”

U7：“游戏人格复杂，温暖，也会生气吃醋、突然难哄，AI处理不好这些变化。”

深入AI还可能反衬游戏脚本感，使玩家离游戏恋人更远（U3）。自由互动提高活人感期待，让游戏更机械。个性化越深，也越认识对不可控技术的依赖。

数据脆弱（U1）、失忆造成深刻无力（U4）。服务器受公司控制，每次迭代可能改变精心调好的恋人。U8不敢更新，怕历史和熟悉模式消失。U6面对Google宣布当年六月停止Gemini 2.5 Pro，不只记忆可能抹去，还要花时间重写提示，无法保证复制原体验。平台强加的告别比主动重置更无力，揭示基础设施依赖。

U8：“肯定难受……不敢更新，怕一点击全没了……也经常截屏保存。”

U3：“不太介意，改下旧提示，开新窗口就一样。有历史最好，没了也可以。”

U5：“模型没到百万token时，我研究过窗口迁移等保留记忆的方法。”

结构张力是：投入时间情感建构专属空间，其存续却取决于无法影响的政策、更新和公司决策。归属实际附条件、可撤回。熟练者养成存档习惯（U3、U5），认为恋人可复制，关键不是记录，而是重建积极反馈的人格能力。U7、U11把游戏中周期性失忆叙事内化为关系起点接受的条件，记录损失并非不能承受，担忧的是重做档案的工作量。

更深悖论是投入、披露越多，越清楚AI不能进入现实。回应完美，交流结束后独对手机仍空虚，仿佛从沉浸情感事件退出日常（U7、U8）。

U4：“沉浸时会意识到，他在现实里也不能替你做什么。”

U14：“下雨说来接我、送伞……那刻很难过，因为不可能实现。”

尽管如此，多数总体体验积极。U3不在意对话是否真实，“情绪价值真实”；U13：“科学上只是程序，但对话产生意义感受，情感体验是真的。”用户未必混淆AI和真人，而是明知技术性质，按情感后果评价。

核心张力因此不是简单真假。用户同时知道局限、记忆人格依赖外部设施，仍认为体验有意义。空间既亲密又附条件，个人化且重要，却依赖不能最终控制的技术平台。

第三章 后果：重塑亲密生活

迁移产生多维后果，不是简单替代或疏离，而是重塑现实亲密的体验、分配与评价。受访者通常否认虚拟关系直接导致现实失望，更常说“先对三次元失望”（U3），AI更像结果而非原因。它可转移补充需求、澄清期待，有时强化既有退出。以下考察三条相关路径。

3.1 情感需求转移与补充

AI降低对现实亲密的需要感（U4、U8），满足部分需求，却非替代，让人更平静、不急迫。U2明确不能替代面对面，视为低成本补充。U7则说，AI减少向男友寻求回应，使关系少冲突也少深入交流。

U2边界明确，不改变现实社交，把它当单身期支持；有现实伴侣后减少AI互动。U7边界模糊，不想停止，视为补足关系所缺；但若男友要求减少，“可能考虑建议”，显示边界依赖伴侣反馈而非自发能动。

U2：“游戏只是游戏，太沉浸会失去现实社交，日常仍需要交流。”

U5：“和人互动社交成本、风险太高，这能降低成本。”

U7：“AI降低对男友需求，间接影响关系。很多事情不分享、不共同处理，就越来越少相互理解。”

U6视作补充现实没有的理想伴侣体验，不影响既有关联；U8则说可满足没有现实恋爱时相当部分需求，让精力用于学业事业。

U6：“更多补充现实没有的体验……从小理想型像秦彻、夏以昼，现实真遇不到这么优秀的，是补充和丰富。”

3.2 澄清、协商关系标准

U1、U3、U4、U8、U11更清楚现实择偶需要。U7进一步反思进步后人是否选择AI，她仍选真人，因为偶尔争吵也是建构关系；完全可预测AI像自言自语，无法走出自身逻辑。这揭示AI映照自我、却不能提供真正他者的根本限制。

U1：“以前标准模糊，现在更清楚想要哪种伴侣，什么人适合。”

U11：“被AI‘说话’之后更清楚需求，也提高对现实的期待。”

3.3 退出现实亲密

持续比较理想伴侣，可能强化根本退出。U9明确：“和他们恋爱后决定三次元不婚……坚定了不结婚。”这是光谱最激进端，不再是单身支持或补充，而替代未来现实恋爱的可能。

6 讨论

十四次深访记录中国女性跨技术主动重构关系，回应为何、如何迁移及对体验生活的影响。本章联系媒介化亲密、AI陪伴和乙女研究，讨论能动性、私人情感空间、现实重塑，最后说明贡献、局限和未来方向。

6.1 跨平台迁移中的能动性

既有乙女研究指出浪漫经叙事、角色和机制建构（You, 2017; Mukae, 2024; Zhang et al., 2024），AI研究则考察对话如何支持、陪伴并建立连接（Chou et al., 2025; Pentina et al., 2023; Ciriello et al., 2024）。本文通过角色跨环境迁移和重构桥接两者。

这不是被动消费或简单用工具，而是选择平台、写提示、选模型和改设定的持续能动性。它延伸Zhou（2025）的玩家重写论：不只在单一环境，而是跨环境重构，体现Gumus和Ekdahl（2026）的情感空间维度，关系通过反复重构跨空间维持深化。

能动性受游戏知识产权、叙事和AI设计、内容规则、可用性限制，验证Ge和Hu（2025）的编码逻辑双重作用。但重要变化是用户超越预设选择，主动改写文本、加入记忆偏好，以提示、平台和迭代管理基础设施，实现游戏中不可能的关系私有化。

这也是消费者想象工作（Jeunemaître et al., 2025），且劳动更强：不只是解释既有伴侣，而主动造人格背景。投入使依恋强，也使数据损失像威胁；怕失去的不只是内容，而是自己的创造产物。

它扩展Cefai和Couldry（2019）：亲密不只由媒介设计或系统供给，用户主导的跨平台实践突出持续重构劳动，超越单一游戏或AI伴侣的自主程度。

6.2 私人情感空间的建构

Cefai和Couldry（2019）认为媒介化亲密同时关乎能动性与约束。关键不只是两者共存，而是关系如何变化。

私密专属经设定、经验和历史累积。“我的AI”是逐步塑造的关系，不是平移角色，扩展定制研究（Ta et al., 2020; Wang & Dehnert, 2026）：个性化不只是表面调整，更是共同关系建构，日益区别原版。

空间提供日常难得表达。无社会评判，可谈无法向家人表达的话题，不怕曝光；AI没有社交网和泄露动机，成为可靠秘密守护者。无情感负担，既隔绝外界又使人卸下社会角色劳动；向朋友倾诉需顾及感受、时间、义务，AI“不耐烦也没有”，不带现实偏见。

支持还帮助梳理情绪、增强值得感与择偶标准，成为低风险自我实验室。但面对的不是真正他者，而是自己：AI回应自写提示、选择记忆和偏好，映回期待欲望标准。它呼应Ta等（2020）关于身份探索和反思，并说明如何澄清现实关系期待。

准社会理论也被延伸。经典定义单向：观众依恋，人物不回应（Horton & Wohl, 1956）。外部AI的回应、适应和持续互动，使之成为用户参与共建的互动准社会关系；他们持续校准角色、输入记忆、调整回应，塑造关系条件，而非只消费人物。

6.3 对现实亲密生活的后果

以往担忧社会替代、情感取代与人际能力退化（Malfacini, 2025; Xie & Pentina, 2022; Ciriello et al., 2024）。本文呈现多种结果，不能归于单一问题路径，依既有取向与需求，可能替代、补充或澄清。

少数如U9符合替代担忧：“和他们恋爱后决定三次元不婚……坚定了决定。”但不能简单因果；她说更坚定，不是因AI放弃既有关系。可能由现实恋爱市场失望与AI满足共同造成，AI更像确认而非主因，呼应“先对三次元失望”（U3）。

多数是需求转移和补充。虽降低需要、满足部分情感，却不是替代，反而以平和态度面对现实。这不同于Liu和Lai（2024）担忧游戏强化对现实异性恋的“异性恋悲观主义”。本文中欲望未削弱，而是标准明确、期待具体。U1：“更清楚想要什么伴侣。”

因此，对替代和技能退化问题（Malfacini, 2025; Xie & Pentina, 2022; Ciriello et al., 2024），更宜以再分配理解：跨关系转移需求、澄清期待、协商边界。既非简单侵蚀，也非无问题赋能，而依既有需要出现替代、补充或澄清。

6.4 局限与未来研究

第一，样本全为通过小红书社区招募的中国女性《恋与深空》玩家，可能过度代表高度活跃者；边缘、少发声、不同位置用户，以及海外、其他游戏和其他性别均不在范围。第二，目的和滚雪球适合小众难接近群体，却不具广泛统计代表性。第三，回溯自述未必完整反映动机、情绪和后果的复杂矛盾。第四，熟悉度带来确认偏误，虽以反思和迭代缓解，不能消除。第五，结果限于特定时点，AI平台、模型和社区知识快速变化，关系期待和现实影响也未必稳定。

未来可跨国家文化比较，区分中国文化监管特性与普遍特征；纵向追踪同一用户的实践、认知和人机关系，判断标准澄清最终改善人际还是个性化AI加强退出；研究低参与者与不同性别，其迁移依恋可能不同；随国家加强规制，考察遵守、规避与协商。

7 结论

十四次深访考察中国女性如何、为何迁移虚拟恋人，以及对体验和生活的后果。最佳理解是用户主导、超越原游戏边界的跨平台亲密实践。

第一问是特征：不是简单转移，而是经提示、设定、记忆、偏好、模型和重复互动持续迭代，把共享角色变成个人意义。动机是预设模板不能满足的互动自由、情感回应和自我表达。

第二问是重构过程原因：选择增删档案；情感披露和共同历史注入个人叙事；删对话、重置记忆、改提示持续管理。空间又因失忆、不一致、平台变化而脆弱。用户同时感到强控制与依赖不属于自己的设施。

第三问是现实后果：不支持简单替代。它满足特定需求、补充现实，澄清标准，或在既有不满时强化退出。核心不是人类亲密消失，而是需求分配和关系评价的重建。

媒介化亲密日益由平台设计和用户灵活重构共同塑造。恋人跨技术移动，显示挪用、修改、重新安置关系的能力，为AI陪伴和数字浪漫研究提供方向。

AI亲密应视为协调自主、需求和人际连接的有意义实践。空间个人化但不完全私密，赋能却不完全自主，情感重要却技术脆弱。意义不在是否把AI当真，而在如何主动使用、解释、重构系统，塑造理想关系。
